Amaca DS / Overview
Start / Overview

Design products that reshape the future.

Motion-first. AI-readable. Built in the open.

Amaca is my personal design system. It started as a side project — a place to practice the kind of system I'd been wanting to build for years (full story here). It's grown into something more specific: a design system where motion is a foundation, not a finish, and where every rule is written so an AI agent can read and apply it as cleanly as a human can.

What's inside

§ 01.1

The system in three layers — hard tokens at the base, components built strictly from them, and the applied patterns that compose both. Each layer cites the one below it, never the reverse.

01 · Foundations08

Hard tokens

The tokens everything else is built from. Color, type, spacing, motion, and the rules that hold them together.

02 · Components39

Build blocks

The primitives I reach for when designing a product surface. Buttons, forms, cards, and the patterns that emerge from them.

03 · Applied07

In practice

How the system performs in practice: the presentation and case study templates, and the guidelines, from the principles to voice and accessibility.

The mark

§ 01.2

The symbol: three isometric cubes in motion forming a triangle, one cube per product. It ships as a fixed asset, and the shell renders it inside the brand tile.

The symbol

Three isometric cubes forming a triangle, in motion.

Each cube is a product. The triangle is a system — components snapping together, breaking apart, reassembling. The motion is intrinsic, not applied: the mark is an animated SVG, one vector file describing every rotation and every transition. The logo follows the same logic as the system itself — written, not decorated.

Start / Documentation

Amaca, packaged for every tool.

Pick your tool, grab the file — or the turnkey .zip — and drop it in. Every download is token-only: it makes any AI reference your tokens by name instead of inventing values. Same source on every surface — the spec is DESIGN.md, the tokens are tokens.css / tokens.dtcg.json. MIT.

How to install

§ 03.1

Per-runtime. Pick the row that matches your tool — the first three mirror the hero cards above.

  1. 01 · COWORK / CLAUDE CODE
    ANY ANTHROPIC RUNTIME

    Install the plugin, or drop the .skill bundle in.

    In Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add angelomacaione/amaca-design, then /plugin install amaca-design@amaca; it installs the skill from amaca-plugin.zip with a SHA-256 pin. In the Claude app: Settings → Capabilities → Skills → upload amaca-frontend.skill. Invoke with amaca-frontend or just describe an Amaca task — the skill auto-triggers on context.

  2. 02 · FIGMA
    — AGENT SKILL

    Install it like the Claude skill, invoke /amaca-figma.

    In any Figma file: prompt box → attachment icon → Skills → Add skill → upload amaca-figma.md. Then /amaca-figma: it fetches the live spec first, generates with Amaca Variables, and self-audits in a verify loop — or audits a selection on canvas evidence. Code-side sync (tokens pushed as Variables over the Figma MCP) stays available through the amaca-frontend skill.

  3. 03 · GOOGLE STITCH
    — DESIGN.MD

    Paste the spec into the project box.

    Download DESIGN.md — the spec ships in the Google Labs design.md standard. On Stitch's Start with your project screen, paste it into the existing DESIGN.md box (or upload the file). Pick the most capable model for brand fidelity.

    Frontier-tier model required. On lighter models the spec is read as passive context, not instructions — see § 03.3 capability tiers.

  4. 04 · CURSOR / VS CODE / WINDSURF · CONTINUE / AIDER
    — EDITORS & ASSISTANTS

    Drop the spec at your tool's rules path.

    Where the editor installs Agent Plugins (Cursor, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, OpenAI Codex, Kiro), install amaca-plugin.zip. Otherwise unzip amaca-ide.zip at the repo root: core + per-target rules, attached only to the files they govern:

    • Cursor.cursor/rules/amaca-core.mdc · amaca-html.mdc · amaca-react.mdc
    • Cursor · Codex (skill).agents/skills/amaca-frontend/
    • VS Code (Copilot).github/copilot-instructions.md + instructions/amaca-*.instructions.md
    • Windsurf.windsurf/rules/amaca.md
    • AiderCONVENTIONS.md
    • Continuerules in config

    The runtime reads it as instructions and grounds on the spec.

    Model-gated — fidelity tracks the model behind the editor. See § 03.3.

  5. 05 · GEMINI ADVANCED
    — GEMS

    Spec as knowledge, instructions as system prompt.

    Create a new Gem. Paste AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md into Instructions: it is self-contained, with the token values inlined. Upload DESIGN.md as the Gem's knowledge file for the full component specs. Save. That Gem now speaks Amaca for any frontend task.

    Frontier-tier model required. On lighter models the spec is read as passive context, not instructions — see § 03.3 capability tiers.

  6. 06 · CHATGPT
    — CUSTOM GPT

    Same pattern as Gems.

    Create a Custom GPT, or a Project. AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md as instructions, DESIGN.md as knowledge file. Same result.

    Frontier-tier model required. On lighter models the spec is read as passive context, not instructions — see § 03.3 capability tiers.

  7. 07 · ONE-OFF
    ANY LLM CHAT

    Attach and prefix.

    Attach AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md to the chat: about seventy lines, every token value inlined, where DESIGN.md runs to thousands. Prefix your prompt with "Use this as the canonical reference for tokens, components, and voice — generate strictly compliant frontend code." Lighter than the skill but works when nothing else does.

    Frontier-tier model required. On lighter models the spec is read as passive context, not instructions — see § 03.3 capability tiers.

  8. 08 · REPLIT / LOVABLE / V0 / BOLT / BASE44
    — APP BUILDERS

    Feed the tokens, not the skill.

    Prompt-to-app builders impose their own stack (usually React + Tailwind + shadcn) and treat a pasted spec as soft context. Give them AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md as project knowledge and, where they take files, theme.css (the Tailwind @theme) as the project foundation — those travel; the enforcement workflow does not. Replit is closest (its Agent reads project files — drop a rules file). Base44 is the tightest (locked stack). Compliance is model- and platform-gated: a frontier model + tokens-as-foundation gets most of the way — verify with the § 03.3 scan.

  9. 09 · NPM · CDN
    — THE WHOLE SYSTEM

    Install the package, versioned.

    npm install amaca-design, then import amaca-design/tokens.css before amaca-design/components.css. With no install, link the same two files from jsDelivr: cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/amaca-design@5/tokens.css. The package also carries theme.css (the Tailwind v4 @theme), tokens.dtcg.json and DESIGN.md. Satoshi loads from www.amaca.design; its files are not in the package.

  10. 10 · SHADCN
    — ONE COMPONENT

    Add one component, with its tokens.

    npx shadcn add https://www.amaca.design/r/button.json writes the component's CSS and an example into your project, with the tokens and the components it uses. No React and no components.json needed. Every item carries its contract in meta.amaca: usage, parts and their tokens, rules, variants. The index is /r/registry.json.

  11. 11 · MCP
    — ASK FOR A COMPONENT

    Let the agent find and install components.

    The shadcn MCP server reads any registry a project names. Turn it on with npx shadcn@latest mcp init --client claude (or cursor, vscode, codex), then add Amaca to components.json: "registries": { "@amaca": "https://www.amaca.design/r/{name}.json" }. Ask in plain words, "add the Amaca card", and the agent searches @amaca, reads the item with its contract and installs it.

  12. 12 · MCP
    — CONNECT BY URL

    Connect any agent, by URL.

    Add https://www.amaca.design/api/mcp as a remote MCP server: a custom connector in Claude, claude mcp add --transport http amaca https://www.amaca.design/api/mcp in Claude Code, the same URL in Cursor or VS Code. No key and nothing to install. The agent lists the components, reads one with its contract and CSS, the tokens, a section of DESIGN.md, and which file to give for each tool.

What's inside the spec

§ 03.2

The DESIGN.md the skill bundles, and the raw download serves, is organized in the Google design.md grammar:

BlockContents
## OverviewHow to use the file, quick reference, token roles in the YAML front-matter.
## ColorsEvery named hex, scale step, gradient, and the 85/10/5 proportion law.
## TypographyDisplay through caption — size, weight, leading, tracking. Family fallbacks.
## Layout · Shapes · ElevationThe 4-px scale, radius steps, shadow specs.
## MotionDurations, easings, the single curve everything rides on.
## ComponentsButtons, forms, cards, badges, navigation, accordion, chat, loader, diagrams, checkbox, select — props, states, do/don't.
## Do's and Don'tsThe five principles, the anti-patterns, and the rules for AI agents. Voice included.
## AccessibilityColor pairs with ratios, focus rules, reduced-motion contracts.
## ChangelogEvery release, top to bottom. Same as § 31.1.

Model capability tier

§ 03.3 · what to expect

The skill encodes a 7-step workflow and 14 verification checks. Whether the runtime model executes them rigorously depends on its reasoning capacity, instruction-following fidelity, and how it grounds on uploaded files.

FRONTIER · RECOMMENDED

Production-grade enforcement.

Claude Opus 4.x, Claude Sonnet 4.x, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro. Explicit tool calls to read DESIGN.md, syntactic token registry checks, gap-surfacing protocol invoked correctly, voice register maintained.

Validated empirically: Gemini 3.1 Pro held strict Amaca compliance on a design-tool runtime.

SCORE · N=4
8.5/10
GAP HANDLING
9.5/10
LIGHTWEIGHT · BEST-EFFORT

Usable output, partial compliance.

Claude Haiku, GPT-5 mini, Gemini 3 Flash. Token references are mostly canonical, principles are cited, structure is sound. Expect two weaknesses:

  • 01Class name proliferation. New classes where canonical components would compose.
  • 02Micro-inconsistencies. Radius drift, occasional minor token substitution, edge cases on multi-component composition.
30-SEC SCAN After any generation, grep the code for hex literals (#XXXXXX instead of var(--color)), raw px values (16px instead of var(--s-4)), raw duration literals (600ms instead of var(--d-*) — ratified continuous loops are the only exception), --ease-spring on effect properties (color, background, opacity, shadow — § 09.3 RIGID), new .classname introductions outside the canonical § 3 registry, and missing @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) overrides. Catches most drift regardless of model tier.
A11Y FLOOR · § 06 Brand-fill text contrast: text on primary-500 (#F051D5) defaults to obsidian-950 — 6.5:1, AA. One ratified exception (v2.6.0, § 6.3): .btn-primary, .badge-solid and .card-feature-tab carry obsidian-050 at ≈2.8:1 — kept on perceptual grounds, scoped to those three selectors. Every other magenta fill — chips, tinted badges, non-button CTAs — stays dark-text.
RUNTIME ARCHITECTURE CAVEAT

Beyond model size, the runtime's file-grounding architecture matters. Anthropic-stack tools (Claude Code, Cowork, Cursor with Claude, Continue with Claude) read uploaded files via explicit tool calls — what you upload is what gets read. Consumer chat tools that abstract file uploads as context embeddings may produce performative compliance: the model announces reading DESIGN.md but the actual grounding is shallow.

For non-Anthropic runtimes the most reliable deployment is the platform's custom-assistant wrapper — Gemini Gems, ChatGPT Custom GPT — where instructions and knowledge files load at session level, not per-message context.

React — native

§ 03.4

Tailwind v4 @theme is native: tokens become first-class utilities (bg-primary-500, rounded-md) straight from tokens.css — no Google spec, no build hack. React is first-class in amaca-frontend v1.1.

UTILITIES
bg-primary-500 · text-obsidian-950 · rounded-md

Every token resolves to a utility class against the same var() chain the CSS surface uses. No CSS modules, no translation layer.

IMPORT
@import "amaca-design/theme.css";

One line wires the full token scale into a Tailwind v4 project. theme.css is a @theme projection of tokens.css — var() aliases, no duplicated literals.

OPTIONAL PROJECTION
design.md / W3C DTCG
tokens.json

The Google design.md / W3C DTCG export stays available as an optional, generated projection for lint, diff, and cross-tool interop — not the thing that unlocks React. Same one-way model: derived from tokens.css, not authored separately.

Versioning & license

§ 03.5

Two SemVer streams, one rule each.

VERSIONING — SPEC

Pinned to the system release — the version in the site header is the version of the spec this page ships. Strict SemVer from v1.2.0 onward — minor bumps for additions, major for breaking renames.

VERSIONING — SKILL

Decoupled from spec version. The skill's own SemVer covers workflow changes — new posture rules, verification checks, deploy targets. v1.2.2 re-bundles on the current spec — multi-target across HTML, React, and Figma — and since v1.2.0 it verifies its own output before handing it over. The in-canvas Figma skill (amaca-figma) versions separately.

CURRENT · v1.3.0 → NEXT · v1.3

§ 01 · Foundations / Color

Magenta on Obsidian, one accent, twelve neutrals.

The palette is built around a single primary accent — magenta — set against a calibrated obsidian neutral scale. Two supporting colors (cyan and petrol) carry secondary emphasis when needed, and four semantic colors are reserved exclusively for feedback. The system is dark-first because most of my product work lives in dark interfaces; the obsidian scale is engineered to carry typographic weight without strain.

Tints · alpha

§ 01.6

A colour with an alpha is a token colour times a tint: color-mix(in srgb, var(--hue) calc(var(--tint-*) * 100%), transparent). Seven steps, shown on --primary-500; an opacity is 0, 1 or a token. A value between two steps snaps to the nearest, the smaller at equal distance.

§ 02 · Foundations / Typography

Satoshi, at every scale.

One typeface carries the whole voice. Light through Black, with a monospace companion for metadata and engineering context. Tight letter-spacing at display sizes, loose leading at body.

Use it when
  • Long-form text left-aligned, at most 80 characters per line.
Use something else when
  • Body text centred or wider than 80 characters → left-align it and cap the measure.

Display scale

§ 02.1

The display end of the scale, display to h6, one Swatch type tile each (§ 3.36): the sample in its class at full size, cropped at the end of the line, then size / leading / tracking and weight. Negative tracking is part of the voice at this size, not a tweak.

Pairing rules

§ 02.4

Numbered rules for combining the scale: tracking bounds, weight pairings, the register mixes that hold. Pair inside them.

Rule 01Headlines always negative track. Never tighter than −4%, never looser than −2%.
Rule 02Mono is metadata only. Timestamps, token names, labels, status — never prose.
Rule 03Italic is for emphasis in running text. Never for UI labels or headlines.
§ 03 · Foundations / Spacing

A 4-pixel grid, held religiously.

Every margin, padding, and gap snaps to a multiple of 4, with one half step for micro gaps. Fifteen steps carry the whole system, from hairline to hero.

Scale

§ 03.1

The spacing scale: a 4px grid from --s-0 to --s-32, with --s-0-5 (2px) under the first step, one Swatch space tile each (§ 3.36): the bar at 1:1 on the 4px grid. Every gap, inset, and rhythm in the system is one of these steps.

Space 0--s-00px
Space 0.5--s-0-52px
Space 1--s-14px
Space 2--s-28px
Space 3--s-312px
Space 4--s-416px
Space 5--s-520px
Space 6--s-624px
Space 8--s-832px
Space 10--s-1040px
Space 12--s-1248px
Space 16--s-1664px
Space 20--s-2080px

Where to reach

§ 03.2

Where to reach on the scale for the common cases — icon gaps, button padding, card rhythm, section breath. The fastest route from a layout decision to its token.

ContextTokenNotes
Inline icon–label gap--s-28px. Always.
Button padding (inline)--s-624px on the default button; --s-4 small, --s-8 large. No block padding: the height is a min-height of --s-8 · --s-10 · --s-12.
Card interior padding--s-624px standard. --s-8 on hero cards.
Subsection vertical rhythm--s-2080px between subsections.
Page top padding--s-1248px below top bar.
Section → section--s-2496px breathing room on long pages.
§ 04 · Foundations / Radius

Soft corners, a short scale.

Radius stays small — 8 to 12 px is the working range. Pills and dots take --r-full; everything else stays on the scale.

Use it when
  • Rectangles inside the 8–12px working range; --r-xl for the hero of a case study, --r-2xl for a hero block.
  • --r-full as a shape, not a size: it makes a pill or a circle (button, chip, switch, radio, avatar, status dots, slider track and thumb, the segmented control's track and thumb, skeleton circle, the key-point dot of a case study, the floating navigation bar).
Use something else when
  • A small rectangle past 16px → it reads as a toy: stay in the working range, or make it a pill.

Radius scale

§ 04.1

The radius scale, --r-none to --r-full, one Swatch radius tile each (§ 3.36): the shape at the token’s radius, 1:1. Sub-4px hairlines are a ratified closed list (§ Shapes in the contract), not scale members.

None--r-none · 0

X-large--r-xl · 16pxCase study hero
2X-large--r-2xl · 24pxHero block
Full--r-full · 999pxPill · circle
§ 05 · Foundations / Shadow

Depth, not decoration.

Shadows are low-key, inset-first, reserved for the hierarchy of surfaces — never for emphasis.

Use it when
  • Depth: an element that sits above another, on the elevation scale.
Use something else when
  • Emphasis → type weight or colour, never a shadow.

Elevation

§ 05.1

Level 0 to 4, the menu shadow, the two brand glows and the three focus rings, one Swatch shadow tile each (§ 3.36): a surface on a section ground, where cards and popovers sit. Elevation on this ground is tonal — an inset highlight over a soft drop — never a hard outline; the rings exist only for focus and are never used as depth.

Level 0--sh-0
Level 1--sh-1Subtle
Level 2--sh-2Card

Level 4--sh-4Modal
Glow--sh-glowPrimary hover
Glow soft--sh-glow-soft

Ring halo--ring-haloFocus · pressables
Ring field--ring-fieldFocus · inputs
Ring field danger--ring-field-dangerFocus · invalid
§ 06 · Foundations / Motion

Motion is feedback, not decoration.

Six durations, five easings. Decel for entrances, Accel for exits, Ease in-out for state changes, Spring for playful reveals, Linear for neutral fades, Draw for data reveals.

Durations × easings

§ 06.1

The motion vocabulary at a glance: five easings and where each belongs, one Swatch motion tile each (§ 3.36). Time runs across, position up; the ball on the right rides the curve at the dot’s height. Decel, accel, ease in-out and linear run on the same --d-base so the curves can be compared; spring rides --d-slow, the overshoot needs the room. Each tile plays three times and rests on the end. The pairing rules and the durations each job usually rides are in § 09.3.

x10350t

x10350t

Duration tokens

§ 06.2

Six duration tokens, each named for a job. Stat count-up is a RIGID rule: numeric stats and KPIs compose from zero to their target riding --d-draw · --ease-decel and land exactly on the final value; under reduced motion they jump straight to it.

TokenmsUse
--d-instant100Hover state, tap feedback
--d-quick200Button states, focus rings
--d-base350Default — most UI transitions
--d-slow600Page enters, panel slides
--d-scene900Hero reveals, orchestrated sequences
--d-draw1200Chart draw-on, count-up, progressive data reveals

Easing tokens & pairing

§ 06.3

The trigger decides the pairing: user-triggered states ride --d-quick · --ease-standard; system-triggered transitions — content entering, leaving, or moving without a direct pointer cause — ride --d-base · --ease-decel. Spatial vs Effects is a RIGID rule: every animated property has a type, and the type gates the easing. Spatial properties — transform, position, size, shape — may use any easing, including --ease-spring. Effect properties — color, background, opacity, shadow — use no-overshoot curves only; --ease-spring on an effect property is off-system, and greppable per line.

TokenCurveUse
--ease-decelcubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)Default for system-triggered transitions — entrances, reveals. The system signature
--ease-accelcubic-bezier(0.7, 0, 0.84, 0)Exits, dismissals
--ease-standardcubic-bezier(0.45, 0, 0.55, 1)Ease in-out, symmetric: user-triggered state changes — hover, press, focus, selected
--ease-springcubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1)Pop-in, delight, overshoot — spatial properties only
--ease-linearlinearNeutral: an opacity with no character, a continuous loop

Motion per component

§ 06.4

Every component that moves documents its motion in one fixed schema — same four columns everywhere, no prose specs. The Motion column accepts token pairs only; the Property column declares the type (spatial / effect) so the rule above is checkable on the row itself; the Reduced motion column uses a closed vocabulary — instant · fade-only · none — recording only how the component lands when the global kill-switch (§ 24.3) fires. Seeded with the site-canonical patterns; every new component ships its rows here — and in DESIGN.md § Motion — in the same release. Continuous loops are a ratified class: they run while the component is mounted, on per-component literal clocks — the --d-* scale describes perceived transitions, not idle rhythm. Mechanical loops ride linear (or steps), never an easing curve; every loop is ratified by its own loop row above, and a loop literal without a row is drift — the raw-duration grep exception covers exactly this list, nothing else.

§ 07 · Foundations / Icon

One hand, sixteen by sixteen.

53 icons, one name each, one grid, one stroke. The album is the whole set.

Use it when
  • Naming an action in an icon-only button, or reinforcing a label beside it: add, close, search, replay.
  • Telling a state apart from its neighbours without colour alone: the warning triangle in an alert, the check in a done step.
Use something else when
  • The picture is the content: a photo, a logo, a map → an image, never an icon.
  • The meaning cannot be guessed from the drawing and there is room → a text label, with or without the icon.
  • A status standing alone → Badge, § 3.14.

§ 07.1

Every icon as a Swatch icon tile (§ 3.36): the drawing 4× on its 16 grid with the 14 live area dashed, then at 16 and 24. The drawing is copied into the markup as it is; a drawing that is not here is not in the system. Component spec: § 3.1 in the contract.

§ 07.5

One rule: copy it from the album.

§ 09 · Actions / Button

Action, ranked.

One primary per screen. Everything else recedes. Five variants × three sizes × states.

Use it when
  • The affirmative action of the screen, as the one .btn-primary.
  • Any action on the current page: submit, save, open, apply.
Use something else when
  • Going to another page or resource → Link.
  • An icon-only button whose glyph is not universal and has no tooltip → a labelled button.

Anatomy and code

§ 09.1

The primary button, part by part, with the tokens that draw each part. Switch to Code for its HTML and the rules of components.css that draw it, ready to copy or download.

1Fill--primary-500pressed --primary-600
2Label--obsidian-050--t-body 500 · --tr-snug
3Edge--bw-1 --primary-500pressed --primary-600
4Boxmin-height --s-10padding 0 --s-6 · gap --s-2
5Shape--r-full
6Shadow--sh-2hover --sh-glow + --sh-3 · pressed --sh-1
7Focus--ring-halooutline --focus-width --obsidian-100 · offset --focus-offset
8Motion--d-quick · --ease-standardtransform --d-quick · --ease-spring
9Disabledopacity var(--opacity-disabled)cursor not-allowed
HTML · CSS
<button class="btn btn-primary">Primary action</button>
.btn{
  display:inline-flex;
  align-items:center;
  justify-content:center;
  gap:var(--s-2);
  font-family:var(--font-sans);
  font-size:var(--t-body);
  font-weight:500;
  letter-spacing:var(--tr-snug);
  line-height:1;
  min-height:var(--s-10);
  padding:0 var(--s-6);
  border-radius:var(--r-full);
  transition:all var(--d-quick) var(--ease-standard);
  border:var(--bw-1) solid transparent;
  white-space:nowrap;
}
.btn:disabled{
  opacity:var(--opacity-disabled);
  cursor:not-allowed;
}
.btn-primary{
  background:var(--primary-500);
  color:var(--obsidian-050);
  border-color:var(--primary-500);
  box-shadow:var(--sh-2);
  transition:all var(--d-quick) var(--ease-standard), transform var(--d-quick) var(--ease-spring);
}
.btn-primary:hover{
  background:var(--primary-500);
  color:var(--obsidian-050);
  border-color:var(--primary-500);
  box-shadow:var(--sh-glow), var(--sh-3);
}
.btn-primary:active:not(:disabled){
  background:var(--primary-600);
  border-color:var(--primary-600);
  box-shadow:var(--sh-1);
  transform:scale(.97);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce){
  .btn-primary:active:not(:disabled){
    transform:none;
  }
}
.btn:focus-visible{
  outline:var(--focus-width) solid var(--obsidian-100);
  outline-offset:var(--focus-offset);
  box-shadow:var(--ring-halo);
}

Rules

§ 09.2

What the contract holds the button to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • One .btn-primary per screen. Everything else recedes.
  • Touch. On a coarse pointer every .btn grows to at least 44px tall and every .btn-icon 44px wide — the § 6 floor. .btn-lg already clears it; dense desktop keeps 32.
  • Focus: dual-ring (white outline + --ring-halo). Never remove outline without re-implementing focus visibility.
  • States: § 3.0.1. default · hover · active · focus-visible · disabled · loading, values in the state index. loading is .is-loading on the button: the label turns transparent but keeps the width, and the loader sits at the centre — its composition is § 3.19's. disabled is the native attribute — <button disabled> — which the CSS reads as :disabled; no class produces it.
  • Pressed (active). A coloured fill darkens toward --obsidian-950: the primary lands on --primary-600 (the palette's pressed step, 4.09 : 1 for its label), the danger fill on 85% --danger. A neutral fill goes one step past its hover; the outline takes the link's pressed magenta; the floating button keeps its translucent fill and darkens its edge. Only the primary moves: it gives to scale(.97) on --d-quick · --ease-spring (L8), and under reduced motion it does not move. Never a lighter fill on press (§ 6.3).
  • Primary label is near-white (--obsidian-050) on --primary-500 — a ratified exception to the § 6 floor (§ 6.3, ≈ 2.8 : 1), kept on perceptual grounds. Scoped to .btn-primary; rest and hover are bounded to --primary-500 (no lighten); pressed darkens to --primary-600. The only other light label on magenta is .badge-solid (§ 6.3); never elsewhere.
  • Label weight is Medium 500 — ratified 2026-06-12 after a 400 / 500 / 700 comparison. Under APCA stroke weight is a contrast input and 700 scores strongest, but at 15px the bold label shifts the button's voice; 500 keeps the register, and the legibility budget is carried by the § 6.3 pairing. Don't bold the primary label for emphasis; don't drop below 500.

Variants

§ 09.3

The button variants, one job each. One primary per screen; everything else supports it.

Floating

§ 09.4

A button that stays on screen while the content under it scrolls: Back in a long page, such as a case study. The fill is translucent and blurred, so the text reads through it, and it takes no height of its own. Scroll inside the frame.

Three months of observation came before a single screen. Every interaction was logged for six weeks, then read against eye-tracking data from the research partners.

The map that came back was clear: most distracted-driving events clustered around three flows. Those three became the targets, and everything else waited until they had shipped and been measured.

Every screen had to read in one glance at arm's length. Type grew a step, labels lost a word, and every state that mattered got its own colour and its own word.

The center stack, the cluster and the companion app read the same tokens, so a change shipped once and landed everywhere.

Sizes

§ 09.5

Three sizes — 32, 40, 48 — and the default is the middle one. Size signals density, not importance: the variant does that.

With icons

§ 09.6

Icon-and-label compositions, leading and trailing, and the icon-only square for toolbars where the meaning is universal. The icon-only button is named by its aria-label; the icon itself is hidden from assistive tech.

Do and don’t

§ 09.7

One primary per screen; the variant says how much it matters.

✓Do

Keep one .btn-primary per screen and let the rest recede; give an icon-only button an aria-label that names the action.

✗Don’t

Bold the label, lighten the primary on hover, or remove the outline without a focus ring in its place.

✓Do

Pick the size for density (32 · 40 · 48) and let the variant carry importance.

✗Don’t

Use a button to go to another page: that is a Link.

§ 10 · Actions / Link

Go there, underlined.

Text that takes the reader to another page or resource. Underlined at rest, because the colour alone is not enough.

Use it when
  • Going to another page, document or resource, in a sentence or on its own line.
  • A reference the reader may want to follow: the spec, the source, the next page.
Use something else when
  • An action on the current page: submit, save, open a panel → Button.
  • A trail of the current hierarchy → Breadcrumb.
  • Switching between views of the same content → Tabs.

The link in running text, part by part, with the tokens that draw each part. Switch to Code for its HTML and the rules of components.css that draw it, ready to copy or download.

2Underline--bw-1 --s-1hover --bw-2
3Motion--d-quick --ease-standard
4Focus--focus-width --obsidian-100 --focus-offset --ring-halo
HTML · CSS
<p>Every value is <a class="link" href="#">derived from a token</a> in the file.</p>
.link{
  color:var(--primary-400);
  text-decoration:underline;
  text-decoration-thickness:var(--bw-1);
  text-underline-offset:var(--s-1);
  border-radius:var(--r-sm);
  cursor:pointer;
  transition:color var(--d-quick) var(--ease-standard),text-decoration-thickness var(--d-quick) var(--ease-standard);
}

  color:var(--primary-300);
  text-decoration-thickness:var(--bw-2);
}
.link:active{
  color:var(--primary-500);
}
.link:focus-visible{
  outline:var(--focus-width) solid var(--obsidian-100);
  outline-offset:var(--focus-offset);
  box-shadow:var(--ring-halo);
}
.link[aria-disabled="true"]{
  color:var(--obsidian-400);
  text-decoration-thickness:var(--bw-1);
  cursor:not-allowed;

Rules

§ 10.2

What the contract holds the link to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Choosing the variant is a rule, not a taste (RIGID). If a sentence or a paragraph holds the link, it is .link. .link-quiet is legal only when nothing around the link is running text. When in doubt, .link: an underline that is not needed costs nothing, a missing one is a WCAG failure. A .link-quiet inside a <p>, an <li> of prose or any element that carries running text is a defect, and check 60 fails it.
  • Colour --primary-400, underlined at rest. The colour alone is 2.1:1 against the body text, under the 3:1 a link needs to stand out without a cue (§ 6 floor #1, WCAG 1.4.1), so the underline is not optional and not hover-only. --info is not a link colour: it belongs to status (§ 3.16).
  • Underline --bw-1, offset --s-1, so it clears the descenders. It thickens to --bw-2 on hover while the colour moves to --primary-300; pressed lands on --primary-500. --primary-600 is reserved for the filled button.
  • No visited state. In an application the colour of a link carries no history, and a second colour would need its own contrast pair.
  • Focus: the pressable ring — outline --focus-width --obsidian-100, offset --focus-offset, --ring-halo, radius --r-sm.
  • The label names the destination. "The spec", never "click here" and never a bare URL; a link that opens a file or another site says so in the label.
  • Disabled is an anchor without href carrying aria-disabled="true": --obsidian-400, cursor: not-allowed. A disabled link is rare; if the destination is not available, prefer plain text.
  • Not a button. A link that triggers an action on the page is a defect: it is announced as navigation and cannot be pressed with Space. Use § 3.6.
  • States: § 3.0.1 — default · hover · focus-visible · active · disabled. Motion: the colour and the thickness on --d-quick · --ease-standard, in the § 8.3 index.

In running text

§ 10.3

Underline 1px at rest, 2px on hover with the lighter colour; pressed lands on --primary-500. Component spec: § 3.7 in the contract.

Every value is derived from a token and not chosen by hand. For the details see the contract specification, section 3.

The link on a card keeps the same rule. Read the case study, or the one not published yet.

Quiet variant

§ 10.4

No underline at rest; it appears on hover and focus. Only for a standalone link, where the position and the label already say it is a link. Inside a sentence the colour is 2.1:1 against the text, and WCAG 1.4.1 fails.

Use it Changelog Specification Repository
Never in running text

In a paragraph use the underlined link, so the reader finds it without hovering.

States

§ 10.5

Default, hover, focus-visible, active and disabled. There is no visited state: in an application the colour of a link carries no history.

Default Disabled

Do and don't

§ 10.6

One rule: a link goes somewhere, a button does something.

✓Do

Put the link on the words that name the destination: "the contract specification", not "click here".

✕Don't

Use a link for an action on the current page. That is a button: a link is announced as navigation and cannot be pressed with Space.

§ 11 · Inputs / Checkbox

Many of many, applied on submit.

A square with a tick. The value commits when the form is sent, never on change.

Use it when
  • Many of many; the value applies on submit.
  • A single opt-in, such as accepting terms.
Use something else when
  • The change applies immediately → Switch.
  • Only one option can be chosen → Radio.

Rules

§ 11.2

What the contract holds the checkbox to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Checkbox and radio are told apart by shape — square with a tick, circle with a dot. Never a tick in a circle, never a dot in a square.
  • The switch is the only one of the three that commits on change. If the change needs a Save button, it is a checkbox.
  • The whole <label> is the hit target; on mobile it must reach 44×44 (§ 6 floor #7) — pad the label, don't grow the box.
  • The focus ring lives on the input, not the label, so the halo traces the control.
  • A radio group has exactly one checked member at all times. A group with none is a defect, not a state.
  • State matrix: § 3.0.1. Motion: § 06.4.

States

§ 11.3

A square with a tick: many of many. The value applies when the form is submitted. Shape carries the meaning before colour does. What separates the three choice controls is when they commit.

Checkbox — many of many

Do and don’t

§ 11.4

Shape first: a square with a tick.

✓Do

Make the whole label the target, at least 44×44 on a phone, and keep the focus ring on the input.

✗Don’t

Put a tick in a circle, or use a checkbox for a change that applies at once: that is a Switch.

§ 12 · Inputs / Radio

One of many, with a default.

A circle with a dot, always in a named group. Like the checkbox, it applies on submit.

Use it when
  • One of many, always in a named group with a default.
Use something else when
  • Several options can be chosen → Checkbox.
  • Four or more options and little room → Select.

§ 13 · Inputs / Switch

On or off, right now.

A track with a knob, and the only choice control that commits on change. If it needs a Save button, it is a checkbox.

Use it when
  • One of two, applied immediately: a setting, not a form value.
  • Turning a preference on or off with instant save.
Use something else when
  • The change needs a Save button → Checkbox.
  • More than two options → Radio or Select.

  • The switch is the only one of the three that commits on change. If the change needs a Save button, it is a checkbox.

§ 13.3

A track with a knob: the only choice control that applies immediately, on change.

Switch — applies immediately
Switch or checkbox?

Do / Don't

§ 13.4

The fill carries the state, never a stroke.

✓Do

Let the fill carry the switch’s state: the quiet track when off, magenta when on.

✕Don't

Put a stroke on the switch track. The fill carries the state; a border makes it read as a checkbox that lost its tick.

§ 14 · Inputs / Slider

A number, by position.

Drag a handle along a scale to pick a value, or two to pick a range. A native range input underneath, so the keyboard, the form value and the screen reader come with it.

Use it when
  • Choosing a number, or a range of two, where the rough position matters as much as the exact value: volume, price, opacity.
Use something else when
  • Fewer than about ten steps → Radio or Select.
  • More than a few hundred steps, or an exact value to type → a number in a Text input.
  • A date or a time → Date picker, Time input.

Rules

§ 14.2

What the contract holds the slider to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Count the steps, not the values. The unit is the step: (max − min) ÷ step is the number of positions. Fewer than about ten → Radio or Select. More than a few hundred, or a value the reader has to hit exactly → a number typed in a Text input. 0 to 100 in steps of 5 is 20 positions.
  • Native underneath. Arrow keys move one step, Page Up and Page Down a larger one, Home and End go to the ends. The value goes with the form under the input's name.
  • A range starts on a selection, not on the whole scale. Each thumb is its own input with its own aria-label ("Minimum price", "Maximum price"), and the pair is a role="group" named by the visible label. The lower thumb cannot pass the upper one; they can meet.
  • The value is always shown. In .slider-value, beside the label; the minimum and the maximum sit in .slider-scale. A slider with no visible value is a guess.
  • The fill is the script's. --p on the input (single), --lo and --hi on the pair (range), as percentages of the scale. Without the script the control still works and the fill is absent.
  • No error state. The value is always inside the scale. A slider that cannot be changed is disabled.
  • Targets (WCAG 2.5.8). The thumb is 20px and the whole 32px row takes the pointer, so a click on the track moves the nearest thumb.
  • Motion. The ring on the thumb changes on --d-quick · --ease-standard, none under reduced motion (§ 06.4).

Single

§ 14.3

A label, the value beside it, the scale under the track. The fill runs from the start to the handle. Arrow keys move one step, Page Up and Page Down ten, Home and End go to the ends. The last one is disabled.

Volume
0100
Disabled
0100

Range

§ 14.4

Two handles on one track, each its own range input with its own name. The lower cannot pass the upper; they can meet. A range starts on a selection inside the scale, not on the whole of it.

Price range
Price range
€0€200
Handles together

€0€200

Do and don’t

§ 14.5

Count the steps, not the values.

✓Do

Set a step that gives between ten and a few hundred positions, show the value beside the label, and name each handle of a range.

✕Don’t

Use a slider for three choices or for a value the reader has to hit exactly, or start a range on the whole scale.

§ 15 · Inputs / Text input

Fields that stay out of the way.

Every field draws its outline at 3:1 against its fill; the focus glow carries the attention load. Labels in mono keep them distinct from content.

Use it when
  • Free text on a single line: a name, a search, a URL.
  • Always with a persistent label; the placeholder is never the label.
Use something else when
  • The answer runs over several lines → the textarea.
  • The answer comes from a known list → Select or Radio.
  • A time or a date → Time input, Date picker.

What the contract holds the text input to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Labels are mono-uppercase, --t-micro, --obsidian-300 — one step lighter than the --obsidian-400 mono register (§ Typography), for legibility over dark fields. Always persistent — placeholder is not a label.
  • Height --s-10, declared. min-height: var(--s-10), block padding --s-2, type --t-small: a single-line field is 40px, the height of the default button beside it (§ 3.6). The height is the token, not a sum of paddings.
  • Helper text is .help; the error variant is .help.error.
  • Error is marked with aria-invalid="true" — the border and the helper text both follow from it. Colour alone never says "error" (§ 6 floor #1).
  • States: § 3.0.1. default · hover · focus-visible · error · disabled · readonly, values in the state index (hover is the field's outline, one step lighter, and the .input-action's; error is not a search state). No state is described in prose here.
  • Icon left. A .icon as a direct child of .input-wrap: decorative (aria-hidden), --icon-sm, --obsidian-300, no click. The field pads --s-8 on the left to clear it.
  • Action right. .input-action: a <button type="button"> last in the .input-wrap, 32px square, --r-sm, --icon-sm, --obsidian-300 and --obsidian-100 on hover. The field pads --s-10 on the right. It carries an aria-label: it has no text. The date picker and the time picker use this same part (§ 3.13).
  • Clear. An .input-action with data-input-clear and the x of § 3.1. It is visible only while the field has a value (:placeholder-shown, so the field needs a placeholder) and hidden when the field is disabled or readonly. Clicking it empties the field, fires input and gives the focus back to the field.
  • Search. The field sits in <form role="search"> with type="search", so Enter submits natively. The browser's own clear button is removed: there is one. A search has no error state: no results is a result and is shown where the results go, never on the field.

Fields

§ 15.3

Text, search and textarea, each with a persistent label and the helper text below. States live in the contract’s state matrix; error is aria-invalid, never color alone.

Shown in case study index cards.
Slug must be lowercase with hyphens.

Search

§ 15.4

The icon on the left says what the field is for; the clear button on the right appears once there is something to clear. Enter submits the form. Type in the first one to try it. A search has no error state: no results is a result, shown where the results go.

Do and don’t

§ 15.5

A label that stays; an error said in words.

✓Do

Give every field a persistent label, and say an error in the helper text as well as in the border.

✗Don’t

Use the placeholder as the label, or let colour alone say "error".

✓Do

Show the clear button only while the field has a value, and show "no results" where the results go.

✗Don’t

Give a search field an error state, or keep the browser's own clear button beside ours.

§ 16 · Inputs / Select

Choices, in one place.

A list of options, a number on a slider or a set of actions, behind one trigger. The panel opens below and flips only when the room runs out.

Use it when
  • Native for a fixed, short list; the custom listbox only when native cannot carry the requirement.
  • Four or more options, or little room on screen.
  • A number set by feel rather than typed, such as a price → the Slider variant.
  • Actions on an item that do not fit on screen → the Menu variant.
Use something else when
  • Two or three options → Radio, all of them visible.
  • A value the person must hit exactly → Text input.
  • A place to go → Navigation or Link.

Rules

§ 16.2

What the contract holds the select to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • aria-expanded on .select-trigger toggles "true"/"false"; open state activates the magenta border + glow (same focus treatment as .input:focus).
  • Keyboard focus on the trigger is the pressable ring, not the field glow: the .input .textarea .select | focus-visible row of the state index does not apply to .select-trigger, which has its own row — a trigger is pressed, not typed into. The magenta border stays, from .select:focus.
  • .select-menu placement is viewport-aware: open below the trigger by default; flip above only when the menu's height does not fit below and above offers more room; max-height = min(240px, room on the chosen side), with internal scroll beyond it — measure the menu's natural height with getBoundingClientRect() rounded up (not scrollHeight, which rounds and skips the border), and scroll only when the menu is really shortened; clamp horizontally to the viewport. The menu never covers adjacent content (e.g. a chat composer the control sits above). Use position:fixed measured from the trigger's rect (.select-menu.is-fixed) when the control may sit near a viewport edge or above important content. A transformed ancestor becomes the containing block of a fixed element, so measure where (0,0) lands and subtract it; position:absolute; top:calc(100% + 4px); left:0; right:0 is acceptable only when there is always room below. Background --obsidian-850 (or --obsidian-900 for an elevated overlay); hidden attribute used to dismiss (do not toggle display directly).
  • The panel never transitions. Its box is measured and written by script at open; under reduced motion the global 0.01ms rule gives every property a transition, and a script that reads the start of one places the panel off screen. .select-menu carries transition:none inside the reduced-motion override (v5.0.0).
  • .select-option[aria-selected="true"] is rendered in --primary-400, with a check after the label (.select-check, the album's check, 14px) in the colour of the text. The check's room is reserved on every row, so labels never move when the choice changes. Hover/focus background is --obsidian-800.
  • Only one menu open at a time — opening one closes any other open .select-menu.
  • Enter/Space/↓ on trigger opens.
  • ↓/↑ navigate options; Home/End jump to the first and last; no wrap from the last to the first. First open lands on the currently selected option (aria-selected="true"), or the first if none.
  • A printable character jumps to the next option that starts with the letters typed (typeahead, 500ms).
  • Enter/Space on focused option commits + closes; trigger receives focus back.
  • Esc closes without committing; trigger receives focus back.
  • Tab from open menu closes and proceeds.
  • Click outside the wrapper closes the menu.
  • A fixed-position (viewport-aware) menu also closes on resize, and on a page scroll that moves the trigger. Its anchored coordinates would otherwise drift from the trigger. Scrolling inside the menu never closes it.
  • Window blur does not auto-close (browser-quirk; leave the menu, let the next click handle it).

Variants

§ 16.3

The native <select> for short lists, the custom listbox when options need a look of their own. The chosen option keeps the magenta text and gains a check after its label; a disabled option stays visible and the arrow keys skip it. Both open below the trigger and flip only when there is no room.

Slider

§ 16.4

A number set without typing it. The field is the same; the panel holds one Slider, with one handle or two, and the field shows the value while it moves. Esc puts back the value the panel opened with.

Groups

§ 16.6

A long list splits into named groups: a heading in the grammar of the label, a full-bleed divider between groups. Typing a letter jumps to the next option that starts with it.

Do and don’t

§ 16.7

A choice stays, an action runs, a number slides. The panel finds its own room.

✓Do

Open the panel below the field and above it only when the bottom edge would clip it; open a kebab at the end of a row inward, aligned to its end. Put a destructive action last, after a divider, and one Slider at most in a panel.

✕Don’t

Pin the panel below a field at the bottom of the screen, or let it cover what the person still needs, such as a composer. Use a Menu to hold a value, mix a Slider with options, or put two Sliders in one panel.

§ 17 · Inputs / Time input

Time, without the native picker.

HH:MM in 24 hours, formatted as you type, bounded so an invalid time cannot be entered.

Use it when
  • A time of day, HH:MM in 24 hours, formatted as it is typed.
Use something else when
  • A date and a time together → pair it with the Date picker.

.tp-wheels::after{

    transition:none;
  }
  .tp-wheel{
    scroll-behavior:auto;
  }
  .input-action{
    transition:none;
  }
}
.tp-wheel-item:focus-visible{
  outline:var(--focus-width) solid var(--obsidian-100);
  outline-offset:var(--focus-offset);
  box-shadow:var(--ring-halo);
}
.tp-popover{
  display:block;
}
.tp-popover{
  position:static;
  margin-top:var(--s-6);
  max-height:none;
  opacity:1;
  transform:none;
  pointer-events:auto;
}

Rules

§ 17.2

What the contract holds the time input to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • maxlength="5" and inputmode="numeric" are required.
  • Optional by default; a context can make it required.
  • No type="time": the native picker does not follow the system.
  • Focus and error follow § 3.10.

Time input

§ 17.3

HH:MM, 24h. Auto-formats as you type — the colon is inserted after the second digit, and each position is bounded so an invalid time is impossible to enter. No type="time": the native picker doesn't respect the system.

Type or pick. Arrow Down also opens the picker.
Required when the field is mandatory and left empty on submit.
DIGIT-BY-DIGIT RULES
H1max 2 H2max 3 if H1 = 2, else 0–9 M1max 5 M20–9
CONTRACT
  • maxlength="5" + inputmode="numeric" are required.
  • The : is inserted automatically — users only type digits.
  • Optional by default; can be marked required per context.
  • Focus & error states inherit from § 11.1.

Do and don’t

§ 17.4

Typed, and formatted as it is typed.

✓Do

Let the field format HH:MM as it is typed, with inputmode="numeric" and maxlength="5".

✗Don’t

Use type="time": the native picker does not follow the system.

§ 18 · Inputs / Date picker

Dates, typed or picked.

A single date or a range, typed digit by digit or picked from the calendar popover.

Use it when
  • A single date or a range, typed or picked from the calendar.
  • Dates near today, where the relation to other days matters.
Use something else when
  • A date the reader already knows, such as a birth date → typed Text inputs, no calendar.

Rules

§ 18.2

What the contract holds the date picker to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • The trigger is a real <input> plus a labelled <button> — never a bare div. The popover is role="dialog" with an accessible name.
  • .is-today and .is-selected are visually distinct on purpose: today is a ring, selection is a fill. When a range end lands on today, the ring is dropped (the fill already says it).
  • Range corners are geometric, not decorative: square in the middle, rounded at the ends, fully rounded when start and end are the same day.
  • Disabled days are <button disabled>, not styled-out divs — keyboard users must be able to tell.
  • State matrix: § 3.0.1. Motion: § 06.4.

Date input

§ 18.3

DD/MM/YYYY, single date. Typed input is digit-by-digit masked (slashes auto-insert) and the trailing icon opens a calendar popover that stays in sync. No native type="date" — the browser picker doesn't respect the system. Optional min/max attributes constrain both the typed value and the picker.

Type or pick. Arrow Down also opens the calendar.
Bound to 2026-05-01 → 2026-12-31.
Not a real date — calendar validation runs on blur, after the mask.
DIGIT-BY-DIGIT RULES
D1max 3 D2max 1 if D1 = 3; if D1 = 0, must be 1–9; else 0–9 M1max 1 M2max 2 if M1 = 1; if M1 = 0, must be 1–9; else 0–9 Y1–40–9
CONTRACT
  • maxlength="10" + inputmode="numeric" required.
  • Slashes are inserted automatically — users only type digits.
  • Real-date check (e.g. 31/02 rejected) runs on blur, not while typing.
  • data-min & data-max in ISO YYYY-MM-DD; both optional.
  • Trailing icon & ↓ on the input both open the picker.
  • Locale: English month/day labels, week starts Monday.
  • Single date only. For range selection, see § 11.4.

Date range

§ 18.4

Two coupled inputs sharing one popover. Two months side-by-side on desktop, stacked on mobile. Click 1 sets the start, click 2 sets the end — clicking before start swaps. Footer presets cover the analytics defaults; the helper line auto-counts inclusive days.

Select start and end. Range count appears here.
SELECTION RULES
  • Click 1 → start. Hover preview shows tentative range.
  • Click 2 ≥ start → commits end.
  • Click 2 < start → swaps (becomes new start).
  • Same-day click twice → single-day range.
  • Esc → cancel pending selection & close.
PRESETS
Todaystart = end = today Last 7 daystoday − 6 → today (inclusive) Last 30 daystoday − 29 → today Last monthfull previous calendar month
CONTRACT
  • Two inputs: data-range-start & data-range-end inside a data-range-group wrapper.
  • Same digit-by-digit mask as § 11.3.
  • Popover anchors to the start input. 580px wide, collapses to 280px stacked under 480px viewport.
  • Helper auto-renders N days (inclusive count) on commit.
  • data-min & data-max on either input bound the whole range.

Do and don’t

§ 18.5

A real input and a labelled button; today a ring, the selection a fill.

✓Do

Pair a real <input> with a labelled button; today is a ring, the selection a fill.

✗Don’t

Build the trigger from a div, style disabled days out instead of disabling them, or open a calendar for a date the reader already knows, such as a birth date.

§ 19 · Feedback / Badge

Small labels, loud signals.

Always Satoshi, always paired with a dot when live. Badges are feedback; they’re never content.

Use it when
  • A status the system computed, next to the thing it describes.
  • The solid variant: the one featured accent of the viewport.
Use something else when
  • A value a person chose → Chip.
  • It needs hover or focus → Button or Chip.

Rules

§ 19.2

What the contract holds the badge to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • The badge's own register. --t-small, weight 500, --tr-snug; padding --s-2 --s-4, gap --s-1; corner --r-md. Line height and case come from the context. It is taller than the Chip on purpose: the badge reports, the chip is handled.
  • A tint is a hue at two strengths, a fill and an edge, text on the full token. The variants use the Chip's pair, --tint-fill / --tint-edge. The default's deep hue, --tertiary-500, uses the heavier --tint-fill-deep / --tint-edge-deep. Never a hand-written rgba.
  • One line, always. A badge never wraps (white-space: nowrap) and never shrinks in a flex row (flex: none): when room runs out, the text beside it wraps instead.
  • The dot (.dot, --s-1 square, --r-full, currentColor) leads every status badge. The solid badge carries none.
  • The solid badge takes the light label, --obsidian-050 on --primary-500: the second ratified exception of § 6.3, bounded like the first.
  • States: § 3.0.1. default only: a badge is static — no hover, no focus. If it needs one, it is a button or a chip.

Status variants

§ 19.3

The badge variants: semantic color plus the dot. Shape and label carry the state; the tint reinforces it.

Default Live Shipped Pending Blocker Archive Featured Info

In context

§ 19.4

Badges in running context — rows, cards, headers — where they annotate a noun rather than announce a state.

Arc Automotive HMI
2024–2025 · 18 months
Shipped
Project Orion — IoT platform
2025–2026 · ongoing
Pending
Field observability
2023 · 6 months
Archive

Do / Don't

§ 19.5

A badge is a label read at a glance; it holds its line.

✓Do

Keep it to a word or two, the status first, on one line beside what it describes.

✕Don't

Let it break onto two lines. When room runs out the text beside it wraps; the badge never does.

§ 20 · Feedback / Chip

A value someone chose.

A chip carries a value a person put there: a filter, a tag, a removable choice. Status the system computed is a badge.

Use it when
  • A value someone entered, chose or can take back: a tag, a facet, a recipient.
  • Pressable chips narrow a set.
Use something else when
  • A status the system computed → Badge.
  • Pressable and dismissible at once → a list row.
  • A link to another page → Link.

Rules

§ 20.2

What the contract holds the chip to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • The variant is a tint, at the Badge's two strengths. Background at --tint-fill (0.08), border at --tint-edge (0.3) — tokens since v4.3.0 — text on the full token — the same pair § 3.14 already uses, so the two small labelled objects of the system read as one family. The neutral chip is the exception and the majority case: --obsidian-800 on --obsidian-700, the card surfaces. A filled chip — solid magenta behind white — is off-system: one filled accent per viewport is the whole 85 / 10 / 5 budget, and a filter row would spend it six times over.
  • A chip may be static. A chip that is neither pressable nor dismissible is legal and is the common case — a tag, a category, a value shown but not editable here. What makes it a chip rather than a § 3.14 Badge is who owns the value: a chip carries something a person entered or chose, a badge reports state the system computed. The affordance follows from the context, not from the definition.
  • --r-full, always. A chip with a rectangular radius is a badge wearing a chip's label. The radius is how the two are told apart at a glance, so it is not a variant.
  • The label rides --t-small. --t-micro is the dense step, legal inside a table cell or a toolbar and nowhere else. No other step is on-scale for a chip.
  • A chip carries at most one affordance, never two (RIGID). Pressable or dismissible, not both. Both roles want the 44×44 target and two of them do not fit inside one 28px object without one swallowing the other. A filter chip is a <button> and the whole object is the target; a tag that leads to the list of its tag is an <a>, pressable the same way, with no aria-pressed and no disabled state; a dismissible chip is static and the dismiss button is the only target. A chip that is both is off-system — that pattern is a list row, not a chip. Carbon reaches the same rule from the other side: "avoid using tags with multiple functions to prevent confusion and reduce accidental clicks". It is a decision, not a law — Calcite and Fluent ship the combination deliberately.
  • The touch target grows, the chip does not. At --t-small the rendered box is shorter than the 44×44 floor (§ 6), so the hit area is extended with a transparent inset pseudo-element. Growing the chip to reach 44px instead makes the densest component in the system the tallest one.
  • A filter chip declares aria-pressed, and a group of them is a role="group" with an accessible name. Selection lands on the border and the text (--primary-500 · --primary-400), never on a magenta fill: a filter row is exactly the place where one filled accent becomes six.
  • The dismiss names its value. aria-label="Remove Motion", never a bare × and never "Remove". Removing a chip changes a collection the reader can't otherwise see change, so the field's own live region announces it — not a toast (§ 3.17 is for things that happened somewhere else).
  • Never colour alone (§ 6 floor #1). The label carries the meaning; the variant is emphasis on top of it. There is no icon-only chip — a chip without a label is a dot.
  • Chips wrap, they never scroll and never truncate. A collection long enough to need either collapses behind a trailing +N chip, which is itself a .chip and a button. A horizontally scrolling chip row hides values from a keyboard and from a screen reader alike.

Chip

§ 20.3

A compact label for one value that belongs to something else — a tag on a post, a facet on a result set, a recipient already entered. Where a badge reports what the system computed, a chip carries what a person chose. Six variants on the badge's tint, an optional dot; most chips are neutral and static.

Design systems Motion Amaca Resolved Needs review Broken link Auto-imported

Filter chips

§ 20.4

Pressable chips narrow a set. Each is a button that holds its state in aria-pressed, and the row is a named group. Selection lands on the border and the label, so a row of six selections still spends no fill.

Removable chips

§ 20.5

Values entered into a field. The chip itself stays static; the dismiss is the only target and its label names the value it removes. The field announces the removal in its own live region, and a long collection collapses behind a trailing count.

Recipients
Angelo Macaione Design team Reviewers

Do / Don't

§ 20.6

The chip is the one object here the reader owns: they put the value there, so they can take it back.

✓Do

Use a chip for a value someone entered, chose or can take back. It may be pressable or removable — one of the two, never both.

✕Don't

Use a chip to report status the system computed: that is a badge, and the giveaway is that nobody can remove it. Or let it break onto two lines: the text beside it wraps instead.

§ 21 · Feedback / Alert

Inline, in context.

An alert states a condition where it applies, and stays as long as the condition is true.

Use it when
  • A condition that applies to the whole surface, inline, as long as it is true.
Use something else when
  • The reader must be able to dismiss it → Toast.
  • It concerns one field → the field's .help.error.
  • Two alerts on one surface → merge them into one.

Rules

§ 21.2

What the contract holds the alert to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • The fill never changes. Every variant sits on --obsidian-850; semantics ride the 2px left rule and the icon. A tinted alert surface would spend the 5% semantic budget on furniture (§ Law, L1).
  • The icon is mandatory and aria-hidden — it is the shape half of "colour never alone" (§ 6 floor #1). The text carries the meaning.
  • role="status" for informative, role="alert" for danger. Nothing else.
  • An alert is not dismissible, at all. Not on a timer (§ 6 floor #6) and not by the reader either: it clears when the condition clears. A close button would let someone hide a state that is still true. If the reader must be able to make it go away, the message is transient and belongs in § 3.17 Toast — that is the whole difference between the two components.
  • Entrance is the system's canonical reveal — [data-alert-fade] + .is-in, opacity plus 12px from below on --d-slow · --ease-decel, the same ride as [data-fade]. Staggered when several land together. Under reduced motion they are simply there.

Alert

§ 21.3

Inline, in flow, addressed to the whole surface. The fill never changes — semantics ride the 2px left rule and the icon, so the accent budget stays spent on actions, not on furniture. An alert is never dismissible — not on a timer, and not by the reader either.

Do / Don't

§ 21.4

An alert states a condition; it clears when the condition clears.

✓Do

Let an alert clear when the condition clears. If the reader has to be able to make the message go away, it was never an alert — it was a toast.

✕Don't

Give an alert a close button. It lets someone hide a state that is still true, and the next reader inherits a screen that lies.

✓Do

Carry the semantics on the left rule and the icon. The surface stays --obsidian-850 in every variant, so the accent budget stays spent on actions.

✕Don't

Tint the fill red or green to say "error" or "success". That spends the 10% band on furniture, and colour alone never carries meaning.

§ 22 · Feedback / Toast

An event, at the edge.

A toast reports something that just happened. It notifies; it is never the record.

Use it when
  • An event that just happened somewhere else.
Use something else when
  • A fourth message in the stack → Alert.
  • It is the only record of the information → keep it somewhere durable.
  • A critical message that needs an action → Modal.

Rules

§ 22.2

What the contract holds the toast to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Auto-dismiss is opt-in and bounded (§ 6 floor #6). data-autohide is permitted only when the toast carries no action and is not .toast-danger; anything with an Undo or an error stays until dismissed. Hover and focus pause any countdown.
  • The region is aria-live="polite"; a .toast-danger carries role="alert" on the toast itself.
  • Newest enters at the bottom of the stack. Three visible at most — a fourth means the surface should be showing an § 3.16 Alert instead.
  • A toast is never the only place a result appears. If losing it loses the information, it wasn't a toast.
  • Same grid as § 3.16: icon and title on the first row, body returning to the icon's left edge below.
  • A toast enters and leaves on the same side it lives on — 24px from the right, opacity with it. Coming in from below would read as the page growing; coming in from the edge reads as something arriving from outside the page, which is what it is. Exit retraces the entry exactly: same axis, same distance, opposite direction.
  • The stack closes the gap, it never snaps. Dismissal is two moves on two curves, and they are not the same move. The toast fades and slides out on --d-quick · --ease-accel — that is the exit. Its box then collapses on --d-base · --ease-decel — and that is not an exit at all: it is the repositioning of the toasts below, which are not leaving, they are settling into a new place. Accel on the collapse would tell the survivors they are being dismissed too. Same roll-off shape as the chat message (§ 3.35). Removing the node outright drops everything below it by a full toast height in one frame — that reads as a glitch, not a dismissal.
  • The two rides differ in speed, not in path. In: .is-in, --d-base · --ease-decel — the system announcing itself. Out: .is-out, --d-quick · --ease-accel — the reader dismissed it, get out of the way. Remove the node after the exit resolves; under reduced motion it goes at once.
  • The toast keeps its close button. It is the dismissible half of the pair: § 3.16 Alert has none by contract.
  • Motion: § 06.4.

Toast

§ 22.3

What an alert becomes when the message is about an action that just happened somewhere else. Transient, stacked bottom-right, three visible at most. Auto-dismiss is opt-in and bounded: only for a toast with no action that is not an error, and hover or focus pauses the countdown.

Do / Don't

§ 22.5

A toast reports an event, and something durable keeps the record.

✓Do

Mirror every toast somewhere durable. A toast is a notification of a result, never the record of it.

✕Don't

Auto-hide a toast that carries an Undo or an error. The countdown races the reader; hover and focus must pause it.

§ 23 · Feedback / Progress

How far, at a glance.

A track and a fill on the primary, drawn on as the value arrives.

Use it when
  • A wait with a known end, longer than about three seconds.
Use something else when
  • A short or unknown wait → Loader.
  • Content arriving into a known layout → Skeleton.
  • Steps the reader takes → Stepper.

Rules

§ 23.2

What the contract holds the progress bar to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Two heights. 8px by default; .progress-sm, 4px, where the bar sits inside a row or a card. Nothing between: 6px is not on the scale.
  • Named and valued. The track carries role="progressbar", aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and a name; the value is also written as text.
  • Known end only. An unknown wait is a Loader; a bar that moves without a value is not a Progress.
  • Motion. On view the fill draws from zero on --d-scene · --ease-decel from 700ms and lands exactly on its value; a new value moves the fill on the same curve. Reduced motion: the fill is at its value.

Progress bar

§ 23.3

The linear meter: draws from zero to its value on view and lands exactly. The value is stated in text beside the bar. Two heights: 8px by default, 4px with .progress-sm where the bar sits inside a row or a card.

Do and don’t

§ 23.4

A known amount of work, with its value written.

✓Do

✗Don’t

§ 24 · Feedback / Loader

The logo, in motion as a promise.

A loader is a contract: something is happening, don't leave. The Amaca logo carries that contract at four scales — inside a button, beside an input, over a card, across the viewport. Under prefers-reduced-motion the animated mark steps aside and a single magenta ring spins in its place.

Use it when
  • A real wait; the large size for full-page waits, the extra-small inline and in buttons.
Use something else when
  • A wait under 200 ms → show the result, no loader.
  • A wait past 800 ms → Skeleton, when the shape of the content is known.
  • Progress is known → Progress.

Anatomy and code

§ 24.1

Rules

§ 24.2

What the contract holds the loader to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Show the loader within 100ms of the action that triggered the wait. Late loaders read as glitches, not feedback.
  • A 200ms wait deserves no loader at all — show the result.
  • One full-page loader per route at a time. After 800ms hand off to a Skeleton.
  • Don't stack a section loader inside a card that already sits inside a full-page loader.
  • Resolve to the success state when a wait completes green. Let the loader keep spinning after the wait is over and you've shipped a bug surface, not a state.
  • Never use the loader as a decorative animation. The mark is in motion because something is loading.

Do / Don't

§ 24.6

A loader has a job. If it isn't communicating a real wait, it's decoration — and decoration on a brand mark dilutes the mark.

✓Do

Show the loader within 100ms of the action that triggered the wait. Late loaders read as a glitch, not feedback.

✕Don't

Pop the loader after the response already returned. A 200ms wait deserves no loader at all — show the result.

✓Do

One full-page loader per route at a time. After 800ms hand off to skeleton frames so the page reads as structurally present.

✕Don't

Stack a section loader inside a card that already sits inside a full-page loader. The user can't tell which wait is which.

✓Do

Pair every loader with an accessible name — aria-label on the loader root or a visible label. Screen readers announce role=status politely.

✕Don't

Use the loader as a decorative animation in the corner of a hero. The mark is in motion because something is loading — never because the page is.

✓Do

Resolve to the success state when a wait completes green — the checkmark crossfades in over the logo on --ease-spring and the live region announces.

✕Don't

Let the loader keep spinning after the wait is over. A loader that won't stop is a bug surface, not a state.

§ 25 · Feedback / Skeleton

The shape of the page, before the page.

A grey placeholder with the size of the content that is coming. When the data lands nothing moves, because the room was already there.

Use it when
  • The shape of the content is known and the wait is past 800 ms: a list, a card, a profile.
  • The content replaces it in the same place and at the same size.
Use something else when
  • The shape is unknown → Loader.
  • A wait under 800 ms → show the result, no skeleton.
  • Progress is known → Progress.

  position:relative;
  overflow:hidden;
  background:var(--obsidian-700);
}
.skeleton-line{
  height:var(--s-3);
  border-radius:var(--r-sm);
}
.skeleton-circle{
  --size:var(--s-8);
  flex:none;
  width:var(--size);
  height:var(--size);
  border-radius:var(--r-full);
}
.skeleton-line::after, .skeleton-circle::after{
  content:"";
  position:absolute;
  inset:0;
  background:linear-gradient( 90deg, transparent 0, color-mix(in srgb, var(--primary-500) calc(var(--tint-fill) * 100%), transparent) 50%, transparent 100% );
  animation:skeleton-shimmer 1600ms linear infinite;
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce){
  .skeleton-line::after, .skeleton-circle::after{
    animation:none;
    opacity:0;
  }
}

Rules

§ 25.2

What the contract holds the skeleton to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • The same size as the content. The shapes take the height and the width of what will arrive, so the swap moves nothing. If the size is not known, the shape is not known: use a Loader.
  • Visible inside a card. The fill is --obsidian-700. --obsidian-800 is the colour of the card and the shapes would disappear.
  • Quiet. The shimmer is a magenta tint at --tint-fill over 1600 ms, linear, in a loop. No high-contrast sweep.
  • Not the only signal. The region carries aria-busy="true" and a name (aria-label). When the content lands, aria-busy goes away and a live region (role="status") says so.
  • Silent shapes. Every shape is aria-hidden="true". A skeleton is never focusable and never a link.
  • Reduced motion. The shimmer is off and the fill stays still (§ 06.4).

Shapes

§ 25.3

A line for text, a circle for a person, a block for an image. The fill is --obsidian-700, so it stays visible inside a card; the shimmer is a quiet magenta tint and stops under reduced motion.

Text
Person
Card

Loading, then loaded

§ 25.4

The region is aria-busy while the shapes are there, the shapes are aria-hidden, and a live region says when the content arrives. The two states have the same height.

AM
Angelo Macaione
Design engineer

Do and don’t

§ 25.5

A skeleton promises a shape; keep the promise.

✓Do

Draw the shapes at the size of the content and announce the end of the wait.

✗Don’t

Use a skeleton for a wait of a few hundred milliseconds, for content whose shape you do not know, or as the only sign that something is loading.

§ 26 · Overlays / Modal

Ask once, clearly.

A window that interrupts the page to ask for a decision or to collect a piece of data. It holds attention until the person answers, which is why it is rare.

Use it when
  • A decision that must be made before the person goes on: confirm a destructive action, answer one question.
  • A short form that belongs to one task: rename, invite, create.
Use something else when
  • A message that needs no answer → Alert or Toast.
  • Content that is long or the person will come back to → a page.
  • An image to look at closely → Lightbox.
  • A menu or text from the edge, with the page still visible behind it → Drawer.

Rules

§ 26.2

What the contract holds the modal to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • The panel is the card's surface, not a new one. Same fill, border and radius; what lifts it off the page is --sh-4 and the --scrim behind it. A modal with a radius of its own is a second card shape.
  • --scrim is a veil. The page stays visible, dimmed and softened by --blur-veil (the Veil material). The Lightbox takes the Bar material, darker and more blurred, because it is a viewer.
  • Open it with showModal(). The browser then traps focus, makes the rest of the page inert, and closes on Esc; none of that is rebuilt. It rides --z-overlay, and the page behind does not scroll.
  • The title is the name. aria-labelledby points at .modal-title. A confirmation that needs the answer to proceed uses role="alertdialog" and aria-describedby on the body.
  • Focus goes to a control, never to the panel. The first control, or for a destructive confirmation the least destructive one (Cancel). On close it returns to the control that opened the modal.
  • Closing (RIGID). Esc always closes. A click on the scrim closes too, except in a role="alertdialog" and whenever the modal holds data not yet saved. The close button is always present, so the way out never depends on a gesture.
  • Actions: one primary, at the end. A destructive action is .btn-danger and is never the default focus. A modal has at most two actions and no third "learn more" link; that goes in the body.
  • Never stack. A modal opened from a modal is a flow that wants a page.
  • Small screens: at ≤480px the panel keeps --s-4 of margin on each side, the actions stack at full width, and the body scrolls inside the panel. A panel anchored to the bottom is a different component and is not this one.
  • Motion. In: the panel fades in and rises --s-2; out: the same, faster. Reduced motion: instant. Rows in the § 06.4 index.
  • No state matrix beyond default. The panel is never focused or pressed itself (§ 3.0.1); the controls inside carry their own states.

Widths

§ 26.3

480px by default; 720px, .modal-wide, for a form of several fields or a table. There is no third width. At 480px and below the panel keeps a margin on each side and the actions stack.

Do and don't

§ 26.5

A modal asks one thing and gives it clear answers.

✓Do

Ask one thing and give it two clear answers, with the primary action last and a destructive one never focused first.

✕Don't

Use a modal for a message that needs no reply. That is an alert or a toast, and it must not stop the person.

§ 27 · Overlays / Popover

More than a hint, less than a window.

A panel anchored to the button that opened it. It holds a link, a short form or a few actions, and the page stays where it was.

Use it when
  • Details about one element that carry a link or a button, and do not need to leave the view.
  • A short form or a choice tied to one control: a rename, a share link.
Use something else when
  • Short text with nothing to click → Tooltip.
  • The content is wider than 360 px, or the person must answer before going on → Modal.
  • A list of actions → a menu.
  • A menu or text that needs the full height of the screen → Drawer.

Rules

§ 27.2

What the contract holds the popover to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • A click opens it, never a hover. Hover belongs to the Tooltip. The trigger is a real button with popovertarget, so the browser sets aria-expanded and the link to the panel.
  • Two kinds of close. A read-only popover is popover (auto): a click outside or Escape closes it. A popover with a form is popover="manual": it closes only on its own buttons and on Escape, so a stray click does not lose the field. Escape on a manual one is handled by the page controller, and the focus goes back to the trigger.
  • One at a time, never nested. An auto popover closes the one that is open. A popover inside a popover is a Modal.
  • Up to 360 px. Wider, or taller than the view, is a Modal. No horizontal scroll.
  • A name. With a title or a form it has role="dialog" and aria-labelledby; a text-only one has aria-label. It is not modal: Tab can leave it.
  • No arrow. The 4px gap and the anchoring point to the trigger, as in the Tooltip.
  • It is placed by CSS. From the invoker, with position-area and a flip when there is no room; no script measures anything. The one exception is the Map (§ 3.43): its popover stays inside the map and beside its cluster, so the map's script places it.
  • Motion. It fades in and rises --s-1 on --d-quick; out, the same, faster. Reduced motion: instant (§ 06.4).

Forms

§ 27.3

A read-only popover is auto: a click outside or Escape closes it. One with a form is manual: it closes only on its own buttons and on Escape, so a stray click does not lose the field. The trigger is a button with popovertarget.

Placement

§ 27.4

Above
