Do and don’t

§ 27.5

A popover is a click away, not a hover away.

✓Do

Open it with a button and give it a name, and let a form popover close only on its own buttons.

✗Don’t

Open it on hover, put a popover inside a popover, or use it for content wider than 360 px.

§ 28 · Overlays / Drawer

From the edge, with the page still there.

A modal anchored to a side: a menu or a piece of text, flush with the edge, the page dimmed behind it. No corners, no frame of its own.

Use it when
  • A menu or a few groups of links that open from the edge: the main navigation on a small screen.
  • Text or details of one item that need the full height: release notes, the facts of a row.
Use something else when
  • A decision to answer before going on, or a short form → Modal.
  • A long form, or work that deserves its own address → a page.
  • A panel that stays beside the page → a layout, not a Drawer.
  • Short text tied to one button → Popover.

Rules

§ 28.2

What the contract holds the drawer to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • A modal, anchored. The modal's surface, padding and scrim; no radius, since it sits flush with the edge. The shadow is one step below the modal's (--sh-3 against --sh-4), so it takes no edge.
  • Open it with showModal(). As the modal: focus is trapped, the page behind is inert and does not scroll, Esc closes, and focus returns to the button that opened it. It has the same data-modal-open and data-modal-close hooks.
  • The title is the name. aria-labelledby points at .drawer-title; the menu is a nav with an aria-label, and the current page carries aria-current="page".
  • Closing. Esc always closes, and so does a click on the scrim, except when the drawer holds data not yet saved. The close button is always present. A click on a link of the menu closes it too.
  • The width is a line. 45 characters plus the padding for text, 30 for a menu, never wider than the screen; at 480px or less it takes the full width.
  • A menu uses the List. The rows are a.list-item of the List, at --t-lead; groups are named with .drawer-label, two levels at most.
  • Not for a form. A short form is a Modal, a long one a page. The drawer is for reading and for choosing where to go.
  • Never stacked, no bottom. A drawer opened from a drawer wants a page; one from the bottom is a different component.
  • A menu opens on the side of its toggle. A toggle at the end of the bar opens it at the end (the default); one at the start uses .drawer-start.
  • Motion. It slides in from its edge on --d-base · --ease-decel and the scrim fades with it; out, the same on --ease-accel. Reduced motion: instant (§ 06.4).
  • No state matrix beyond default and current. The panel is never focused or pressed (§ 3.0.1); the rows carry the List's states.

Release notes

v5.0.0 re-architects the components one at a time: each one is approved on a render before anything is written to the repo.

Slider, Divider, Skeleton, Popover and Drawer are new. Text input gains an icon and an action.

Breaking

The date and time pickers lose .dp-icon-btn in favour of .input-action.

Migration guide

The wide drawer holds text with longer lines: a guide, a diff, a table of renamed classes. It keeps the same edge, the same scrim and the same motion; only the width grows, to 60ch plus the padding.

Read it top to bottom, then close it and the page is where you left it.

Do and don’t

§ 28.4

The drawer is for reading and for choosing where to go.

✓Do

Use it for a menu or a text the person reads with the page still behind it, and name it with its title.

✗Don’t

Put a form in it, stack one drawer on another, or make it a panel that stays on the page.

§ 29 · Overlays / Tooltip

A label, on demand.

Opens on hover and on focus, one at a time. It labels a thing already on screen; it never holds anything the reader must reach.

Use it when
  • A label for something already on screen.
  • Only on interactive elements, such as an icon-only button.
Use something else when
  • The information is needed to finish the task → .help or Alert.
  • It needs a title → Alert.
  • It holds a link or a button → Popover.

Rules

§ 29.2

What the contract holds the tooltip to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Opens on hover and on focus. A tooltip reachable only by pointer fails § 6 floor #5.
  • At most one tooltip is open at a time (RIGID). Opening one closes every other — two bubbles on screen overlap, and an overlapped label is a label that can't be read. Escape closes; scrolling closes. This cannot be expressed in CSS (:hover has no memory of the others), so the open state is the .is-open class and a controller owns it. A tooltip that opens on a bare :hover rule is off-system.
  • The trigger references it with aria-describedby; the bubble is role="tooltip". A tooltip with no trigger relationship is decoration.
  • No interactive content. No links, no buttons, no form controls — there is no accessible path to reach them.
  • Never the sole carrier of meaning (§ 6 floor #1). If the information is required to complete the task, it belongs in .help or in an § 3.16 Alert.
  • No arrow. The 6px offset and the anchoring do the pointing; an arrow adds a shape to maintain at every edge case.
  • Plain text only, one or two lines. A tooltip that needs a title is an alert.

Tooltip

§ 29.3

A label for something already visible. Never a container for content, never the sole carrier of meaning. Opens on hover and on focus — a tooltip reachable only by pointer fails the accessibility floor. The last one opens below and aligns its end to its anchor: near the top edge and the end edge, the bubble stays on screen.

Pushes local tokens to the Figma library Rebuilds every download bundle that embeds a changed file Pending Waiting on a review before it can ship

Do / Don't

§ 29.4

A tooltip labels a thing already on screen.

✓Do

Keep one tooltip open at a time, opened on hover and on focus. Two bubbles on screen overlap, and an overlapped label cannot be read.

✕Don't

Put a link, a button, or anything required inside a tooltip. There is no accessible path to reach it, and it disappears the moment the pointer leaves.

§ 30 · Navigation / Navigation

Wayfinding, un-decorated.

Top nav for marketing. Sidebar nav for dense documentation (this system uses its own). Breadcrumbs in mono — always.

Use it when
  • The sidebar for documentation; the top bar for marketing.
  • The sidebar when there are more than five destinations.
Use something else when
  • A linear journey with an order → Stepper.

Rules

§ 30.2

What the contract holds the sidebar and the top bar to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Flush, and translucent. No radius, no shadow on scroll. The bar wears the Bar material with a fading edge: the page scrolls under it blurred, and the bar ends in a mist rather than a line.
  • The item is the target. Each item takes the full height of the bar, so the target is 48px wide-open (§ 6 floor #7).
  • States. On a translucent bar a fill would read as a block over the blur, so the item never fills: hover lightens the label to --obsidian-050, pressed dims it to --obsidian-300 while it is held. The current page is --primary-400 at weight 600, with no underline and no fill: the weight is the second cue, since the magenta against --obsidian-200 is 1.44:1 (WCAG 1.4.1). data-label repeats the label so its bold width is reserved and selecting an item never moves its neighbours.
  • Focus inside. The ring is drawn inside the item, as on the List's row, so the bar clips nothing.
  • It reads its own width. The bar is a size container: at 720px of its own width or less (--bp-md) the destinations and the action leave and the toggle appears. The same markup works in a page, a frame or a panel.
  • The menu opens on the toggle's side. The toggle opens the Drawer menu (.drawer.drawer-nav, § 3.24) with showModal(); a toggle at the end opens it at the end, one at the start uses .drawer-start. The action moves into the drawer's foot.
  • The glyph sits on the inset. The toggle is pulled out by the space around its 16px glyph, so the icon lines up with the brand's edge on the other side.
  • States: § 3.0.1. default · hover · active · current · focus-visible on the item; the action and the toggle are Buttons and carry the Button's rows: disabled · loading included (§ 3.6).
  • Motion. Colour on --d-quick · --ease-standard; reduced motion: instant (§ 06.4).
  • The Bar material, its line all round, lifted. --surface-bar under --blur-bar, a 1px --border-subtle line on every edge, --sh-3, --r-full. No fading edge: the pill has an edge of its own.
  • Wide: one pill at the top. As wide as its content, centred, sticky --s-4 from the top, at most the page width less --s-8. Brand, destinations and the action sit in it.
  • The brand mark loses its tile in both forms: the logo and its glow, no fill and no edge (§ 3.5). A square tile in a pill reads as a stranger.
  • At --bp-md or less: a row and a pill. The bar becomes a plain row that scrolls away with the page, holding the brand and the action; the destinations float in a pill fixed --s-4 above the bottom edge and above the safe area (env(safe-area-inset-bottom), Safari's bottom toolbar), centred. The page keeps the pill's room at its foot (--s-12 + --s-8), so its last line is never under the pill. It reads the viewport, not its own width: the pill belongs to the screen the thumb holds.
  • One markup. The nav stays where it is in the document, after the brand and before the action; the CSS moves it. Reading and tab order do not change between the two forms, and nothing animates between them: a device sees one.
  • At most five destinations, and no toggle. Each keeps its label. A site with more destinations uses the flush bar and its Drawer menu.
  • Always on screen. The pill does not hide on scroll: on a phone the browser's own toolbar already comes and goes.
  • States. The item's, as on the flush bar: hover lightens the label, pressed dims it, the current page is --primary-400 at 600, the ring is drawn inside the item.

Floating bar

§ 30.4

The same bar lifted off the page. Wide, one pill at the top with the brand, the destinations and the action; on a phone, the brand and the action stay at the top of the page and the destinations float in a pill at the bottom, where the thumb is. Two real pages at two widths: scroll each one. Component spec: § 3.26 in the contract.

Do and don’t

§ 30.5

A few destinations, one action, the current page marked.

✓Do

Keep it to the brand, a few destinations and one action, and mark the current page with aria-current.

✗Don’t

Round the flush bar or lift it off the page (that is the floating bar), underline the current item or open its menu on the side opposite the toggle.

✓Do

Keep the floating bar to five destinations with their labels, and leave the page room at its foot for the pill.

✗Don’t

Move the nav in the markup to place the pill, hide the pill on scroll, or put the action in the pill on a phone.

§ 31 · Navigation / Tabs

One view, several panels.

Tabs switch panels in place, and the indicator travels to the selected tab.

Use it when
  • Related views of one page, read one at a time.
Use something else when
  • Moving between pages → Navigation.
  • A linear process → Stepper.
  • The reader needs several sections open at once → Accordion.

Rules

§ 31.2

What the contract holds the tabs to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Panel swap is fade only: never crossfade, never slide both. The leaving panel is removed (display:none) before the new one fades in.
  • Keyboard: Tab reaches each trigger; Enter/Space activates.
  • One indicator. One .tab-indicator per tablist, 2px of --primary-500, moved with transform and width; never an underline per tab.
  • Views of one page. Tabs switch what one page shows; going to another page is Navigation.

Tabs

§ 31.3

Tabs with one shared indicator that travels — 2px of magenta, transform-driven. The panel swaps as the indicator lands.

Tab content sits in the active panel. Indicator is a 2px magenta underline that slides between tabs. Inactive tabs stay at tertiary weight.
The process panel. Three months of in-vehicle observation, instrumentation of the legacy HMI, and correlation with eye-tracking data before a single screen was drawn.
The outcome panel. −41% task time, +12pt retention, 94% token adoption across 7 surfaces in 18 months.
The reflection panel. Under‑invested in the companion mobile app for the first 6 months. Correcting course late cost us a quarter of rework.

Do and don’t

§ 31.4

One view at a time, one indicator that travels.

✓Do

Fade the new panel in once the old one is gone, under one magenta indicator that travels.

✗Don’t

Crossfade or slide both panels, or use tabs to move between pages: that is Navigation.

§ 32 · Navigation / Segmented

Two views, one thumb.

A pill of two or three segments switches the view in place, and one thumb travels to the selected segment.

Use it when
  • Two or three views of the same content, switched in place: the anatomy and the code of a component, a chart and its table.
Use something else when
  • Views of different content, or more than three → Tabs.
  • Moving between pages → Navigation.
  • A value the reader submits with a form → Radio.

  width:0;
  background:var(--obsidian-700);
  border:var(--bw-1) solid var(--border-input);
  border-radius:var(--r-full);
  box-shadow:var(--sh-1);
  transition:transform var(--d-base) var(--ease-decel), width var(--d-base) var(--ease-decel);
  pointer-events:none;
  will-change:transform,width;
}
.segmented-panel{
  opacity:0;
  transform:translateY(6px);
  transition:opacity var(--d-quick) var(--ease-standard), transform var(--d-quick) var(--ease-standard);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce){
  .segmented-item, .segmented-thumb{
    transition:none;
  }
  .segmented-panel{
    transition:none;
    opacity:1;
    transform:none;
  }
}

Rules

§ 32.2

What the contract holds the segmented control to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • States: § 3.0.1. default · hover · active · selected · focus-visible, values in the state index.
  • The thumb is the selection. Its edge, --border-input on --surface-sunken, reads at 3.27 : 1 (WCAG 1.4.11); without the edge the fill alone is 1.24 : 1. The label of the selected segment is --obsidian-100 (12.57 : 1 on the thumb), the others --obsidian-300 (6.30 : 1 on the track).
  • One stop on Tab. The selected segment carries tabindex="0", the others -1. Arrow Left and Right select the neighbour and move the focus to it, Home and End go to the ends.
  • Two or three segments, each an icon and a label. The label stays: an icon alone does not say which view it opens.
  • The thumb travels under 120px between neighbouring segments, so it rides --d-base (Motion, duration by distance).

Full width

§ 32.3

With .segmented-fill the segments share the width of their container in equal parts, for a narrow column or a phone.

The anatomy of the component: the track, two segments with an icon and a label, and the thumb under the selected one.
The code of the component: the HTML of the example, its CSS and the tokens it reads, ready to copy.

Segmented control

§ 32.4

Two views of one component, its anatomy and its code. The thumb travels to the segment you pick and the panel fades in as it lands; the arrow keys move between segments. Component spec: § 3.28 in the contract.

The anatomy of the component: the track, two segments with an icon and a label, and the thumb under the selected one.
The code of the component: the HTML of the example, its CSS and the tokens it reads, ready to copy.

Do and don’t

§ 32.5

Two or three views of one thing, each named.

✓Do

Keep two or three segments, each with an icon and a label, under one thumb that travels.

✗Don’t

Drop the labels, put more than three views in it, or use it for a value a form submits: that is a Radio.

§ 33 · Navigation / Breadcrumb

Where you are, in mono.

The path back to the top, in the mono register — always.

Use it when
  • A hierarchy deeper than two levels.
Use something else when
  • A flat site → Navigation alone.
  • Progress through a flow → Stepper.
  • As the only navigation → it sits beside Navigation, never instead.

Rules

§ 33.2

What the contract holds the breadcrumb to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Mono uppercase --t-caption · --tr-mono, gap --s-2. Crumbs --obsidian-300, .sep --obsidian-500, .active --obsidian-100.
  • In the shell topbar the crumbs are static labels — plain spans, no links. A breadcrumb that navigates wraps anchors in <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> and marks the current page with aria-current="page".
  • A crumb that is a link hovers --obsidian-100, presses --obsidian-400 and takes the pressable ring; the current page stays a span.
  • ≤480px: only .active survives — crumbs and separators hide, and the register drops to --t-micro.

Breadcrumbs

§ 33.3

Breadcrumbs in the mono register: the path recedes, the current page is lit. The first two are static labels, as in the shell; the third navigates: its crumbs are links that light on hover and take the focus ring. Component spec: § 3.29 in the contract.

Work/Case studies/Arc Automotive HMI
Journal/2026/On systems that outlive the work

Do and don’t

§ 33.4

Beside the navigation, never instead of it.

✓Do

Wrap a breadcrumb that navigates in <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> and mark the current page with aria-current="page".

✗Don’t

Use it as the only navigation, or to show progress through a flow: that is a Stepper.

§ 34 · Navigation / Pagination

Many pages, always one place.

Links between the pages of one set of items. The current page is marked, the first and the last are always there, and the rest is a gap.

Use it when
  • Pages of similar items too long for one page: search results, a list of case studies.
  • The rows of a table that do not fit on the screen, in the compact form below it.
Use something else when
  • A linear journey such as a form → a Continue button and a Back link.
  • Only one page → show nothing.
  • Content that sits on one page without slowing it → no pagination.

Rules

§ 34.2

What the contract holds the pagination to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • What to show. The first page, the last page, the current page and one on each side; a gap stands for the rest. A gap never sits at an end, and a gap for a single page shows that page instead. Under --bp-sm use the compact form; the numbered one still fits there, as icons without their words, but it is the fallback.
  • The current page is marked, not hidden. aria-current="page" on its link, with the fill and the border of § 3.0.1. It stays a link.
  • Name every link (WCAG 2.5.3). A number carries aria-label="Page 6". Previous and Next carry rel="prev" and rel="next", and their arrows are decorative.
  • The ends stay in place. On the first page Previous is disabled, on the last page Next is: aria-disabled="true" and no href, so the row does not move and the link is not a target.
  • Pages are addresses. Each page is a URL that loads without script. The page number goes in the document title ("Search results, page 6 of 12"), and a page that no longer exists goes to the first.
  • Not for a journey, and not scrolling forever. A form or any linear journey takes a Continue button and a Back link. Infinite scroll takes the keyboard away from the reader; it is not a replacement.
  • Motion. Hover and focus change the background and the colour on --d-quick · --ease-standard, none under reduced motion (§ 06.4).

Numbered

§ 34.3

First, last, the current page and one on each side; a gap stands for the pages in between. Previous and Next stay in place and go disabled at the ends, so the row does not move.

Do and don’t

§ 34.5

One set of pages, one nav.

✓Do

Mark the current page with aria-current, name every number (“Page 6”), and put the page number in the page title.

✕Don’t

Use it for a form or any linear journey, show it for a single page, or replace it with infinite scroll.

§ 35 · Navigation / Stepper

Step by step, in order.

A linear progress indicator for multi-step flows: forms, onboarding, checkout.

Use it when
  • A linear flow: forms, onboarding, checkout.
  • Three or more steps.
Use something else when
  • Fewer than three steps → a Next button.
  • Steps that can be done in any order → Tabs.

HTML · CSS
<nav class="stepper stepper-vertical" aria-label="Checkout"><ol class="stepper-list"><li class="stepper-step is-done"><span class="stepper-dot"><svg class="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path d="M3 8.5l3 3 7-7.5"/></svg></span><span class="stepper-text"><span class="stepper-label"><span class="stepper-sr-only">Completed: </span>Cart</span><span class="stepper-meta">Done</span></span></li><li class="stepper-step" aria-current="step"><span class="stepper-dot">2</span><span class="stepper-text"><span class="stepper-label"><span class="stepper-sr-only">Current: </span>Payment</span><span class="stepper-meta">Now</span></span></li><li class="stepper-step"><span class="stepper-dot">3</span><span class="stepper-text"><span class="stepper-label">Review</span><span class="stepper-meta">Next</span></span></li></ol></nav>
.stepper{
  --stp-dot:var(--s-6);
  --stp-cur:var(--s-8);
  container-type:inline-size;
}
.stepper-list{
  list-style:none;
  margin:0;
  padding:0;
  display:flex;
}
.stepper-step{
  flex:1 1 0;
  min-width:0;
  position:relative;
  display:flex;
  flex-direction:column;
  align-items:center;
  text-align:center;
  gap:var(--s-2);
}
.stepper-step::after{
  content:"";
  position:absolute;
  top:calc(var(--stp-cur) / 2);
  left:50%;
  width:100%;
  height:var(--bw-2);
  background:repeating-linear-gradient(90deg,var(--obsidian-300) 0 var(--s-1),transparent var(--s-1) var(--s-2));
  transform:translateY(-50%);
}
.stepper-step:last-child::after{
  display:none;
}
.stepper-step.is-done::after{
  height:var(--bw-2);
  border:0;
  border-radius:var(--r-xs);
  background:var(--grad-progress);
  box-shadow:var(--sh-glow-soft);
}
.stepper-dot{
  position:relative;
  z-index:1;
  width:var(--stp-dot);
  height:var(--stp-dot);
  margin:calc((var(--stp-cur) - var(--stp-dot)) / 2) 0;
  border-radius:var(--r-full);
  display:grid;
  place-items:center;
  font-size:var(--t-caption);
  font-weight:600;
  color:var(--obsidian-300);
  background:var(--obsidian-800);
  box-shadow:inset 0 0 0 var(--bw-1) var(--obsidian-300);
}
.stepper-step.is-done .stepper-dot{
  background:var(--primary-500);
  box-shadow:none;
  color:var(--obsidian-950);
}
.stepper-step[aria-current="step"] .stepper-dot{
  width:var(--stp-cur);
  height:var(--stp-cur);
  margin:0;
  background:var(--grad-progress);
  box-shadow:var(--sh-glow);
  color:var(--obsidian-950);
  font-weight:700;
}
.stepper-step[aria-current="step"] .stepper-dot::after{
  content:"";
  position:absolute;
  inset:calc(-1 * var(--s-1));
  border-radius:var(--r-full);
  box-shadow:0 0 0 var(--bw-1) var(--primary-500);
  animation:stepper-pulse 2400ms var(--ease-standard) infinite;
}
.stepper-text{
  display:flex;
  flex-direction:column;
  align-items:inherit;
  gap:var(--s-0-5);
}
.stepper-sr-only{
  position:absolute;
  width:var(--s-px);
  height:var(--s-px);
  padding:0;
  margin:calc(-1 * var(--s-px));
  overflow:hidden;
  clip:rect(0,0,0,0);
  white-space:nowrap;
  border:0;
}
.stepper-label{
  font-size:var(--t-small);
  font-weight:400;
  color:var(--obsidian-300);
}
.stepper-meta{

  font-size:var(--t-micro);
  letter-spacing:var(--tr-mono);
  text-transform:uppercase;
  color:var(--obsidian-300);
}

  color:var(--obsidian-100);
}
.stepper-step[aria-current="step"] .stepper-label{

  color:var(--primary-200);
}

}
.stepper[data-reveal] .stepper-step::after{

  transform-origin:left;
}

}
.stepper[data-reveal] .stepper-text{

}
.stepper-vertical .stepper-list{

}

}

}
.stepper-vertical .stepper-dot{

}

  top:calc(var(--stp-cur) / 2);
  left:calc(var(--stp-cur) / 2);
  width:var(--bw-2);
  height:calc(100% + var(--s-8));

}

}
@container (max-width: 480px){

    gap:var(--s-8);
  }
  .stepper-step{

  }

  }

  }

    top:calc(var(--stp-cur) / 2);
    left:calc(var(--stp-cur) / 2);
    width:var(--bw-2);
    height:calc(100% + var(--s-8));
    background:repeating-linear-gradient(180deg,var(--obsidian-300) 0 var(--s-1),transparent var(--s-1) var(--s-2));
    transform:translateX(-50%);
  }

  }

    transform:translateY(-50%);

Rules

§ 35.2

What the contract holds the stepper to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Horizontal while the labels fit. Three to five steps with short labels, from 480px of the stepper's own width. Below 480px it turns vertical by itself (a container query); .stepper-vertical forces the column for long labels or more steps.
  • One current step. Exactly one aria-current="step"; done steps before it, upcoming steps after.
  • Done is drawn, upcoming is dashed. The connector after a done step is --grad-progress at --bw-2; the one after the current and upcoming steps is a dashed --obsidian-300 line, 4px dashes and 4px gaps (--s-1) (5.6 : 1 on a card).
  • Contrast. Upcoming labels and every meta line are --obsidian-300 (5.6 : 1 on --obsidian-800); the number and the check on a filled dot are --obsidian-950 (6.5 : 1 on --primary-500).
  • Not a control. The steps are not links: going back is the flow's own Back button.
  • Motion. On view, every dot scales in on --d-slow · --ease-spring (opacity on --ease-decel) and its text rises 8px, from 520ms plus 80ms per step; each connector draws to the next dot on --d-slow · --ease-decel from 580ms plus 80ms per step, done or dashed alike, so the choreography holds for any number of steps. The current dot breathes: a 1px ring scales to 1.33 and fades, 2400ms, in a loop. Reduced motion: everything in place, the ring still.

Horizontal

§ 35.3

Done steps carry a check and a drawn connector, the current step breathes, upcoming steps stay outlined. The current step is announced: aria-current="step" and a hidden word for each state.

Checkout · order flowStep 3 of 5
  1. Completed: Cart2 items
  2. Completed: ShippingExpress
  3. 3Current: PaymentIn progress
  4. 4ReviewPending
  5. 5DonePending

Click to re-trigger animations.

Vertical

§ 35.4

The same steps in a column. It is automatic below 480px of the stepper’s own width, and forced with .stepper-vertical anywhere.

Checkout · order flow.stepper-vertical
  1. Completed: Cart2 items
  2. Completed: ShippingExpress
  3. 3Current: PaymentIn progress
  4. 4ReviewPending
  5. 5DonePending

Click to re-trigger animations.

Do and don’t

§ 35.5

Horizontal while every label fits on one line; vertical when they don’t. One ladder for the reveal, whatever the state.

✓Do

Use the horizontal stepper for three to five steps with short labels, from 480px of width up; let it turn vertical below, or force the vertical one for long labels or more steps.

✕Don’t

Squeeze a horizontal stepper until its labels wrap, hide the labels to make it fit, or show more than one current step.

✓Do

Reveal it on one ladder: dot n scales in from 520ms + 80ms·n, the connector that leaves it draws from 580ms + 80ms·n, both on --d-slow. Done or upcoming only changes the paint, so one more step is one more rung.

✕Don’t

Time the done and the upcoming steps as two phases, hold one back until the other ends, or start the ladder from the current step: the reveal would change every time the person moves on.

§ 36 · Containers / Card

Containers with metadata bones.

Every card carries a micro-header with context — project code, date, index. The case-file influence sits here, quietly.

Use it when
  • One project or one stat: micro-header, title, body, at most one action.
  • A concept the reader scans and acts on as one unit.
  • A list of items, each opening its own page → the row card.
  • The one item a page leads with → the feature card, once per page.
Use something else when
  • Secondary information shown on demand → Popover or Modal.
  • A gradient background → never; the surface stays on the obsidian ramp. The light of the feature card is a glow behind the content, not a fill.

Do and don’t

§ 36.7

One micro-header, at most one action.

✓Do

Give every card a micro-header and at most one action, last on its own row.

Put a gradient on a card, or a .btn-primary unless the card is the screen's single primary act.

§ 37 · Containers / Accordion

Disclosure, on demand.

For dense reference content where users scan headers first and read selectively. Single-open by default; chevron rotates 90° on expand. Keyboard-operable, prefers-reduced-motion safe.

Use it when
  • Dense reference content: headers scanned first, read selectively.
  • Multi-open sparingly, when answers are compared side by side.
Use something else when
  • Content the reader will read in full → a page with headings.
  • Switching quickly between sections → Tabs.

Rules

§ 37.2

What the contract holds the accordion to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Single-open by default.
  • Chevron rotates 90° on expand.
  • Keyboard-operable: aria-expanded toggled, Enter/Space opens/closes.
  • States: § 3.0.1. default · hover · active · expanded · focus-visible on the trigger, values in the state index. Focus is the system's pressable ring, drawn inside the row.

Each part and its rule

Each part of the accordion with the rule that governs it — hit target, single control, chevron direction, duration by measured height.

PartRule
.acc-triggerFull-row hit target — minimum 56px tall. Entire row is a single button; never put a separate toggle inside.
.acc-chevronRotates from 0° (closed) to 90° (open) over 320ms on the standard ease. Color shifts to primary-400 on open. No swap-icon.
.acc-numOptional. Mono index in the form NN / NN. Use when the set has a fixed, ordered count; omit on FAQ-style lists.
.acc-panelAnimates via grid-template-rows 0fr → 1fr — no JS height measurement. Body fades in 80ms after the row starts opening.
aria-expandedRequired on every trigger. Toggled in JS in lockstep with .is-open. The panel carries role="region" and an id referenced by aria-controls.
Reduced motionUnder prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, the row swaps instantly — no rotation, no fade, no grid transition.

Default · single-open

§ 37.3

Used inside case-study briefs and project requirements lists. Opening one panel closes the others — keeps the eye anchored. First item is open on mount so the surface never reads as inert.

Clean informative text that is displayed only when someone wants to deep dive more. Crucial to cluster topics under the same group.

Ship the platform as a living surface, not a release. Feature-flag everything; let production teams roll out capabilities to fleets in cohorts without redeploying the console.

Workstations run 10–14h shifts under variable lighting. Type stays at 16px minimum; primary actions clear AAA contrast on every surface; error states never rely on hue alone.

Every OTA action — operator, target VIN range, package hash, timestamp — is logged and exportable. The interface surfaces this trail in-context, not in a separate compliance tool.

Multi-open · FAQ

§ 37.4

When users compare answers side-by-side. Add data-multi on the wrapper — items toggle independently. Use sparingly; default to single-open.

Yes — typically as a 12–16 week engagement with embedded engineering pairing. I don't ship throwaway redesigns; the system has to outlive my involvement.

Two weeks for a discovery sprint — research, audit, a short written direction. Anything shorter doesn't leave room to disagree with the brief, which is usually where the work is.

Remote-first, with on-site weeks for kickoff and major milestones. I'm based in Milan and travel comfortably across EU.

Do and don’t

§ 37.5

Headers scanned first, one panel open.

✓Do

Open one panel at a time by default, each header a real button with aria-expanded.

✗Don’t

Fold away content the reader will read in full: that is a page with headings.

§ 38 · Containers / Divider

One line, where the topic changes.

A hairline between two blocks of one container. It carries no space of its own: the container sets the gap on both sides.

Use it when
  • A change of topic inside one container: two blocks of a card, a modal or a menu.
  • Groups side by side that need a boundary: the groups of a toolbar.
Use something else when
  • The rows of a List or a Table → the row's own hairline.
  • Space already separates the blocks → no line.
  • The sections of a page → a heading and space.

Rules

§ 38.2

What the contract holds the divider to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • A break, not decoration. The horizontal divider is an hr: a change of topic, with the implicit role separator. A line that only decorates is not a Divider: the rows of a List and a Table already carry their own hairline.
  • The vertical one names itself. A div has no meaning, so it carries role="separator" and aria-orientation="vertical". The parent has a definite height or is a flex row.
  • The labelled one is content. It has no role="separator": that role makes its children presentational and the word would be lost to the screen reader. The two lines are pseudo-elements.
  • The space belongs to the container. No margin on the divider: the gap on both sides is the parent's (--s-4 to --s-6), like the icon's.
  • One weight, one colour. --obsidian-700, 1px. --border-subtle (--obsidian-800) vanishes inside a card, which is --obsidian-800; a heavier line is a different component, not a thicker divider.
  • Static. No hover, no focus, no motion.

Forms

§ 38.3

Horizontal is an hr; vertical is a div with role="separator" and aria-orientation; the labelled one is two lines around a word and is not a separator, so the word stays readable.

Do and don’t

§ 38.4

A line is a break, not decoration.

✓Do

Draw it where the topic changes, and let the container give the space on both sides.

✕Don’t

Put one between the rows of a List or a Table, stack lines to make a heavier one, or add a margin to the divider itself.

§ 39 · Containers / Chat

Conversations that earn their bubbles.

A chatbot interface lives or dies on cadence. Bubbles land with a small spring overshoot, typing indicators promise a reply, and the conversation never overcrowds the surface — older messages roll off after three exchanges. Own bubbles use --primary-700 (deep brand), so --primary-500 stays reserved for CTAs and focus.

Use it when
  • Conversational interfaces: a chatbot, an assistant.
Use something else when
  • A one-way notice from the system → Toast or Alert.
  • Reference content the reader consults, not a dialogue → a page or Accordion.

Rules

§ 39.2

What the contract holds the chat to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Own bubbles fill with --primary-700 — the deep brand accent.
  • The brighter --primary-500 is not used here. It stays reserved for CTAs and focus rings, so the 85/10/5 budget holds in long conversations.
  • A previous "hot last" rule (paint only the latest own bubble primary-500) was tried and discarded — the bright last bubble started reading as a CTA, stealing weight from the actual primary action on the page.
  • One avatar per streak. The rest of the streak uses .chat-avatar-spacer for column alignment, never repeats the avatar.
  • Bot reply replaces the typing bubble in place (mutate the existing .chat-stack, swap .chat-bubble content) so layout doesn't shift.
  • After ~3 exchanges, roll older messages off the top so the surface never overcrowds — under reduced motion .is-out still hides (instantly), per the motion table.

Motion spec

Every transition resolves to a token, in the canonical § 09.4 grammar. Two-stage bubble entry: the container scales from 0.92 with an --ease-spring overshoot (spatial only — the opacity rides --ease-standard), then the inner content fades up 80ms behind.

TriggerProperty (type)MotionReduced motion
message enter · container .chat-bubblescale 0.92→1 (spatial)--d-base · --ease-springinstant
message enter · containeropacity (effect)--d-base · --ease-standardinstant
message enter · content .chat-bubble-contentopacity (effect) · translateY 3px→0 (spatial)--d-quick · --ease-standard · delay 80msinstant
roll-off .chat-msg.is-outopacity (effect) · translateY −8px (spatial)--d-quick · --ease-accelinstant — still hides
roll-off .chat-msg.is-outmax-height + margin collapse (spatial)--d-base · --ease-accelinstant — still hides
typing dots .chat-dot (loop)translateY 0→−4px→0 (spatial) · opacity 0.3→1→0.3 (effect)--d-slow · --ease-standard · stagger 0/160/320msnone — the dots hold still at full opacity
send idle → ready .chat-composer-sendbackground + color (effect)--d-quick · --ease-standardinstant

Do / Don't

§ 39.5

Anti-patterns surfaced from early chatbot builds. Most are 85/10/5 violations dressed up as enthusiasm.

✓Do

Own bubbles fill with --primary-700 — the deep brand accent. Bright --primary-500 stays reserved for CTAs and focus rings.

✕Don't

Paint own bubbles with --primary-500. The bubble starts reading as a CTA and the actual primary action on the page loses its weight.

✓Do

Anchor the typing indicator inside a bot bubble — same shape, same surface, same column. The reader's eye stays where the next message will land.

✕Don't

Float "Amaca is typing…" as a gutter caption below the conversation. For a single-bot UI it's noise; the avatar already says who's typing.

✓Do

Show the avatar only on the first bot bubble of a streak. The rest of the streak gets a 32px invisible spacer so the column stays aligned.

✕Don't

Repeat the avatar on every bot bubble. It hijacks the eye and steals the budget from content.

✓Do

Roll older messages off the top after the conversation passes ~3 exchanges. Fade up + collapse in --d-quick on --ease-accel.

✕Don't

Let the demo grow unbounded. A demo that fills the viewport buries the motion you're trying to document.

§ 40 · Data display / Swatch

A token, shown, not pressed.

A sample of a token: a square of colour beside the word that names it, one step of a palette or of a scale (type, space, radius, shadow), an album icon on its grid, or the curve of an easing at the duration it rides. The value comes from a token, the border keeps a dark colour visible on the page, and nothing about it is interactive.

Use it when
  • A label names a colour: a legend key, a token in a table.
  • A palette shows its values, one tile per step.
  • An easing token shows its curve and the duration it rides, one tile per token.
  • A foundation page shows its scale: type, space, radius, shadow, the icon album, one tile per token or drawing.
Use something else when
  • The colour stands for a state, with a word → Badge or Chip.
  • The shape carries the meaning, not the colour → the Diagrams legend.
  • The user picks a colour → off-system: stop and ask.

Rules

§ 40.2

What the contract holds the swatch to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Static. No hover, no focus: a swatch is not a button and not a picker. Choosing a colour is off-system. The colour forms never move.
  • The motion tile moves because the motion is its value. Time across, position up, as in CSS Easing L1 and MDN: a curve copied from the tile is the curve it shows. The dot rides the curve and the ball on the rail shares its height. The move lasts exactly --d, inside a cycle of 2.5 × --d; three cycles and it rests on the end, under 5 s even on --d-slow (WCAG 2.2.2). It plays when it comes into view, and again each time it comes back. A Replay button under the tiles plays them again; a loop for ever is not an option (WCAG 2.2.2 would then ask for a pause control). Reduced motion shows the end.
  • The curve is set on the element. animation-timing-function: var(--e) on each mover; a var() inside @keyframes is not read and every curve falls back to ease.
  • The radius tile is 1:1, the icon tile is 4×. A radius is judged at its size; an icon is judged on its grid, so the zoom shows where the drawing sits in the 14 live area, and the 16 and 24 beside it show it at size. The zoom is the album drawing in an .icon, never a redrawing.
  • A type tile prints what its class renders. Size, leading, tracking and weight are read from the .ty-* class the sample wears, not typed beside it.
  • A row of examples thins, it does not wrap. .swatch-grid-4 holds four tiles in one row and drops the last ones as its own width shrinks (container query on the bp tokens): 4, then 3 under 900px, 2 under 720px, 1 under 480px.
  • The value is a token. --sw is set to var() of a token, never a pasted hex; --e and --d to var() of an easing and a duration. --sw-r to var() of a radius token, --sw-s to var() of a spacing token, --sw-sh to var() of a shadow or ring token. On a tile the printed hex, radius, curve and milliseconds are that token's value in tokens.css, and the drawn path is its curve.
  • Always bordered. An inset 1px of --border-input, so the size does not change and a dark colour still has an edge: 3.38, 3.27 and 3.13 : 1 on --surface, --surface-sunken and --surface-field (WCAG 1.4.11). On --surface-raised it is 2.93 : 1, so on a card the label is what carries the colour.
  • Before its label. The gap is the container's (a legend row --s-3, a token in a table --s-1); swatch and label are one unit that never breaks across lines.
  • The word carries the meaning. A swatch never stands for a state or a series alone: the label names it (§ 6 floor #1).
  • Named once. Beside a visible label it is aria-hidden="true"; alone, role="img" with an aria-label that names the colour.
  • The Diagrams legend is not a swatch. Its key shows a node's shape, with a border in the colour of the state (§ 3.44).

Forms

§ 40.3

Inline, 12px, before its label; the label names the colour, so the swatch is hidden from the screen reader, and the gap is the container’s. Tile, one step of a palette with its name, the token’s value and its role. Both carry an inset 1px of --border-input. Type tile and space tile, horizontal: a row of their scale, the sample or the bar at 1:1, a divider, the specs. Radius and shadow tiles: the shape at the token’s radius, a surface with the token’s shadow. Motion tile, one easing token on the standard graph: time across, position up, the ball on the rail at the dot’s height; three plays, then it rests on the end (WCAG 2.2.2). Icon tile, an album drawing 4× on its grid.

Do and don’t

§ 40.4

A swatch shows a value; the word next to it carries the meaning.

✓Do

Put it before its label, let the label name the colour, and take the fill, the curve and the duration from tokens.

✕Don’t

Make it a button, let the colour carry the meaning alone, paste a hex or a cubic-bezier where a token exists, loop a motion tile for ever, or stretch the hex swatch out of a regular hexagon.

§ 41 · Data display / Avatar

Who it is, in a circle.

A picture, two initials or a glyph, always a circle, with a name the screen reader can say.

Use it when
  • Showing who a person, team or account is, beside their name or standing for it: a comment, a list row, a menu header, a member list.
  • Several people share one item and a count is enough: a stack of up to five.
Use something else when
  • A picture of a thing rather than of a person or account: a product, a place → an image in a Card.
  • A count or a status standing alone → Badge.
  • An icon that stands for an action → an icon-only Button, § 3.6.

Anatomy and code

§ 41.1

Rules

§ 41.2

What the contract holds the avatar to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Always a circle (RIGID). There is no square variant, and the shape never means "person" or "organisation". A team or an account is told apart by its image or its initials, not by its corners.
  • The name sits on the wrapper (RIGID). role="img" with aria-label="Anna Rossi"; the image has alt="" and the initials are aria-hidden. Next to the name in text the whole avatar is aria-hidden="true", so the name is read once. An avatar with no name and no text beside it is a defect.
  • Image, then initials, then the glyph. The image fails over to the initials by itself (onerror="this.remove()" in the markup, no script of the system). With no name there is the user icon of § 3.1 at 60% of the side, --obsidian-300. Initials are at most two letters.
  • Neutral by default. Every avatar starts on --obsidian-700. The five .avatar-hue-* tints are for telling people apart in a long list, assigned by the caller from a stable key such as the id, never by position and never reshuffled. --danger is not one of them: it reads as an error.
  • A 1px edge on every variant, the image included, so a dark photo and a light one weigh the same on a dark page.
  • Status is never colour alone (WCAG 1.4.1). The offline dot is a hollow ring, and the status goes in the accessible name: "Anna Rossi, online". The ring around the dot is the surface the avatar sits on: set --avatar-ring on a card (--obsidian-800); the default is the page, --obsidian-950.
  • Groups. Overlap is a quarter of the side, and each avatar is cut out of the one before by --bw-2 of the surface, so it works on any background. The last avatar sits on top. Show at most five slots; past that the fifth is "+N", the same size, labelled "N more people".
  • Interactive only when it goes somewhere. An <a> or a <button> carries .avatar and its label names the destination ("Open Anna Rossi's profile"). Hover moves the edge to --primary-400, pressed to --primary-500, focus is the pressable ring. Any other avatar does not react.
  • Motion. The edge colour on --d-quick · --ease-standard — a row in the § 06.4 index; reduced motion is instant.
  • No other states. The avatar is not disabled, selected or loading; a pending picture shows the initials.

§ 41.3

The image gives way to the initials by itself, and with no name there is the glyph. Every avatar starts neutral; the five tints are for telling people apart in a long list.

Do and don't

§ 41.8

One rule: an avatar names someone.

✓Do

Give the avatar a name the screen reader can say, on the wrapper, and hide it when the name is already beside it.

✕Don't

Use an avatar as decoration, or for a thing that is not a person or an account. A picture of a product is an image in a card.

§ 42 · Data display / List

Many things, one row each.

Rows in a column: many things of one kind, or the facts of one. A hairline between rows, nothing around them.

Use it when
  • Many things of one kind, each a line or two, to scan or open: projects, settings, people.
  • The facts of one item as label and value pairs, with an action beside a value to change it.
Use something else when
  • Several columns to compare or sort → Table, § 3.39.
  • A choice from a fixed set → Select or Radio.
  • Bullets inside running text → a plain ul or ol in the prose, no component.

Rules

§ 42.2

What the contract holds the list to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • A row is one thing. Every row of a list has the same parts in the same order; a row that needs more columns is a Table row, § 3.25. A list is not nested inside a row.
  • Static or interactive, by the element. A div row has no hover and no pointer. An a or a button row has hover, focus-visible and disabled (aria-disabled="true"), values in § 3.0.1. The whole row is the one target: no link around a row that holds a button.
  • Name every action (WCAG 2.5.3). An icon-only action in a row carries an aria-label that says which row (More actions for Arc). A text action keeps its visible word at the start of its name (Change owner).
  • Summary semantics. dl with a div per row is valid HTML; each dt has at least one dd. A fact without a value is not a row.
  • The hairlines stay. They tie each row to its action and help the reader who zooms. Drop them only in a list with no actions, and then for the whole list.
  • One density. One row height; there is no small or large list. A list that has to be denser is a Table.
  • Motion. Hover changes the background on --d-quick · --ease-standard, none under reduced motion (§ 06.4).

Items

§ 42.3

One row per thing: a lead (icon or avatar), a title with its meta line, and an end (badge, action, chevron). A static row is a div; a row that opens something is an a or a button and gets hover and focus. The last row here is disabled.

§ 42.4

The facts of one item: a key in mono, a value, and an action beside the values that can change. A key is never empty and neither is a value. Under 720px the three columns stack.

Do and don’t

§ 42.5

One row is one thing.

✓Do

Keep the same parts in every row of a list, and give an icon-only action in a row its own accessible name.

✕Don’t

Put columns in a row to compare them (that is a Table), nest a list in a row, or wrap a whole row in a link and put a button inside it.

§ 43 · Data display / Table

Rows that read in one pass.

Quiet lines, numbers in tabular figures, labels in the mono register.

Use it when
  • Content, not chrome.
  • Comparing values across rows and columns.
Use something else when
  • Laying out a page → Grid.
  • Key facts about one item → List.

  color:var(--obsidian-200);

  }

Rules

§ 43.2

What the contract holds the table to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • No zebra striping. The row rule carries the scan; a second device would double the noise.
  • Left-align everything, including numbers, unless the column is a pure quantity — then use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums and align right.
  • The header is a label, not a heading: mono-uppercase, same register as .label (§ 3.10).
  • A table wider than its container scrolls in a wrapper, .table-scroll (overflow-x: auto) — never shrink the type to fit.
  • Tables are content, not chrome: a row has no state. A row that is a link holds one .table-row-link, the anchor in its first cell, whose hit area covers the row: the row then hovers --obsidian-850, presses --obsidian-800 and takes the pressable ring. One link per row and nothing else pressable in it: a second target would sit under the first.
  • Sorting: one driver (RIGID). A column that sorts holds a .table-sort button in its header. One header drives the order and carries aria-sort; it sits a step lighter and shows its direction. Every other sortable header shows sort-ascending, the order its first click gives.
  • A click never clears the order. On the driver it flips ascending and descending; on another column it makes that column the driver, ascending. The table opens sorted, its driver declared in the markup.
  • The whole header is the target. The button fills the cell, so the target is the header's height and width, never the icon alone. Focus is the pressable halo with the outline inside the cell (offset -2px, as the date picker's days): the frame clips the halo on the table's outer edges, the outline always shows.

Table

§ 43.3

The plainest data surface in the system, and the one this documentation leans on most. No zebra striping — the row rule carries the scan, and a second device would double the noise. The header is a label, not a heading: mono-uppercase, the same register as a field label.

PartTreatmentNote
Frame--obsidian-800 border, --r-mdOverflow hidden, so the radius clips the first and last rows
HeaderMono 10px on --obsidian-850Uppercase, --obsidian-400, weight 500
Cell13px, padding --s-3 --s-4Left-aligned, including numbers
Row rule1px solid --obsidian-800The last row drops it
Inline code.table codeMono 12px, --primary-400
Secondary cell.mutedThis column, throughout

Pure quantities are the one exception to left alignment: align them right, set tabular-nums.

Sortable

§ 43.4

A column that sorts holds a button in its header, and the whole header is the target. One header drives the order: it carries aria-sort, sits a step lighter and shows its direction. Every other sortable header shows the ascending icon, the order its first click gives. A second click on the driver flips it; the table opens sorted and a click never clears the order.

Linked rows

§ 43.5

A row that opens a page is the link: one anchor in its first cell, whose hit area covers the row. The row lightens on hover, a step more while pressed, and takes the focus ring as a whole. A row that is not a link has no state.

Do and don't

§ 43.6

One rule for sorting: there is always a driver. One target per row.

✓Do

Open a sortable table already sorted, with its driver named by aria-sort and a step lighter.

✕Don't

Let a click clear the order, put the sort on the icon alone, or mark the driver by its colour only.

✓Do

Make a row that opens a page one link, its anchor in the first cell covering the row.

✕Don't

Highlight a row that is not a link, or put a second link or button in a linked row.

§ 44 · Data display / Charts

Charts that respect the surface.

Dark canvas. One accent hue per chart. Grid lines at 8% opacity. Numbers in Satoshi, axis labels in mono.

Use it when
  • Bars for comparison, labelled at the value; the donut for composition.
  • Lines for trends over time and for several series.
  • Areas for cumulative totals.
Use something else when
  • Several time series → lines, not bars.
  • Five points or fewer → bars, not a line.

Rules

§ 44.2

What the contract holds the chart card to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • Text is HTML, never inside the svg (RIGID). Every label of a plot (axes, values, a donut's centre) is an element over the drawing, positioned in % of its viewBox and sized by a token, so it reads the same at every width. A <text> inside a plot scales with the drawing and is never a token: 10 units were 14px on a desktop card and 4px on a phone.
  • Two drawings, one shown. A plot whose proportions or points do not hold on a phone carries a second drawing, .chart-plot-sm, with its own viewBox (344 wide against 700), the same data and points at data-r 8; under --bp-md it replaces .chart-plot-lg, labels included. The small one is aria-hidden: the chart has one accessible name. The baseline clip reads its width from data-clip-w.
  • Bars keep two columns down to --bp-md (.chart-grid): one column at 900 made each bar chart twice its size.
  • The plot is not interactive. No hover, no focus, no state but default (state index). A value the reader needs is written as text: the bar label, the legend percentage, the stat.
  • Choreography E (the line and area plot). Each part starts when the one before it reads, not when it ends: the baseline at --d-base, the line --d-slow later, area and points --d-slow after the line starts, the points --d-quick apart. Under reduced motion every part lands drawn.

Do and don’t

§ 44.7

Text over the drawing, timing from tokens, nothing to press.

✓Do

Write every label of a plot as HTML over the drawing, sized by a token, with the same margin on all four sides of the canvas.

✗Don’t

Put a <text> inside the svg, or let a label touch the edge of the canvas.

✓Do

Give a plot that does not hold on a phone a second drawing, and keep the bars in two columns down to 720px.

✗Don’t

Let a phone shrink the desktop drawing until its points and labels cannot be read.

✓Do

Start each part of the reveal when the one before it reads, with every duration, curve and delay from a token.

✗Don’t

Type a duration or a delay by hand, or give the plot a hover or a focus.

✓Do

Give every slice its legend row, with its percentage written.

✗Don’t

Let colour carry a slice alone, or paste a hex where a palette token exists.

Time, laid end to end.

§ 45.2

It scrolls; it never shrinks.

✓Do

Let the plot scroll sideways under the width its lanes need, keep the labels at their tokens, and end the last date on the last gridline.

✗Don’t

Shrink the gantt to fit a phone, write its labels inside the svg, or let a date run off the canvas.

§ 46 · Data display / Maps

Places, on a hex grid.

Places on a grid of hexes: the land is grey, and a cluster takes the colour of its state.

Use it when
  • The pattern in the data is geographic.
  • A few places carry a state; the rest of the land is context.
Use something else when
  • Data for only a few areas → a bar chart.
  • Geographic data with no geographic pattern → another chart.
  • Exact values to compare place by place → Table.

Geographic · hex map

§ 46.1

The land is Natural Earth 1:110m (public domain), baked into the page as a grid of hexes: no request at run time. A coastal cell draws smaller, by how much of it is land. A cluster of cells is one place with nodes: it takes the colour of its worst state, and the rest of the land stays grey. Hover, focus or a click act on the whole cluster, never on one hex: it glows in its colour, and grey land lights its country. The sea never takes a colour. On a wide screen a click opens the cluster's Popover inside the map, beside the cluster, and the rest of the land dims; under 720px a tap opens its Drawer.

Do and don’t

§ 46.2

The cluster is the unit; the sea is never coloured.

✓Do

Act on the whole cluster: it glows in its colour on hover and focus, and a click opens its Popover.

✗Don’t

Scale the cells, light one hex alone, or colour the sea.

✓Do

Keep a few clusters on land that stays grey, each in the colour of its worst state and named in the legend.

✗Don’t

Colour every place, or let a colour carry a state with no legend.

✓Do

Open the Popover inside the map, beside its cluster, and dim the rest of the land while it is open. Under 720px, open the Drawer instead.

✗Don’t

Let the popover leave the map or cover its cluster, or open a popover on a phone.

§ 47 · Data display / Diagrams

Structure, drawn on the same grid.

Flowcharts and system maps from a textual source — auto-laid-out, then themed entirely from tokens. The library only ever sees values read off :root at runtime, so there is no hardcoded hex anywhere: the single source of truth stays tokens.css. Everything is neutral obsidian; exactly one magenta node marks the narrative entry. On scroll, nodes cascade in, then the edges that connect them.

Use it when
  • Flowcharts and system architecture, box and line with grouping.
Use something else when
  • Sequence, tree or ER diagrams → out of scope.

Rules

§ 47.2

What the contract holds the diagram to, word for word from its section of DESIGN.md.

  • One diagram per figure; the source lives in <template class="diagram-src"> and never renders as raw text.
  • Theme only from tokens read at runtime. A hex literal in themeVariables is a regression (§ 9).
  • Exactly one magenta focus node per diagram (:::focus). More than one = decorating (§ 1.4).
  • Semantic state only when a node encodes a real state — color + shape + label + legend (§ 6 #1).
  • Orthogonal routing, soft elbows. Never diagonal. Never CSS transforms on SVG <g> (§ 7.3).

Flowchart · node-edge

§ 47.3

Decisions and paths. Rectangles are steps, diamonds are gates, dashed edges are loops. One magenta node — the entry — anchors where to start reading. Everything else recedes to obsidian.

System architecture · grouped

§ 47.4

Box-and-line with grouping. Subgraphs become clusters — --obsidian-850 fill, --obsidian-700 border — so related boxes read as one zone. The one magenta node is the source of truth every surface derives from.

Semantic states · legend

§ 47.5

The one case for color beyond magenta. When a node encodes a real state, it carries the semantic hue — but never alone: every state node also changes shape and spells the state in its label (§ 6 floor #1). A legend maps each pairing.

Token map

§ 47.6

A <figure class="diagram"> wraps a .diagram-canvas[role="img"] (holding the rendered SVG) and a .diagram-caption. Surface, border, and radius are coherent with .card. Semantic-state diagrams add a .diagram-legend.

ClassRole
.diagramFigure shell. --obsidian-900 surface, 1px --obsidian-700 border, --r-lg, --s-6 padding — the .card frame.
.diagram-canvasRender target. Carries role="img" + a descriptive aria-label; the library injects the SVG here. A textual source sits in a <template class="diagram-src"> until render.
.diagram-captionMono micro, --obsidian-400, FIG-NN · title — echoes .card-meta. The index tints --primary-400.
.diagram-legendOptional. Only on semantic-state diagrams. Each row pairs a shape swatch + a written label — color never carries meaning alone.

Token map — applied through themeVariables populated from getComputedStyle(:root), plus classDef strings built from the same tokens at runtime. The theming config holds zero hex literals.

Motion spec

§ 47.7

Entrance reuses the system's established reveal patterns — nothing new, in the canonical § 09.4 grammar. An IntersectionObserver fires once (threshold 0.15, rootMargin 0px 0px -8% 0px, unobserve after fire); nodes cascade in, then edges and clusters. Opacity only: transforms on the generated SVG <g> groups compose with the cascade and break the auto-layout positioning. The hook runs after the async render resolves, not on first paint.

TriggerProperty (type)MotionReduced motion
enter viewport · nodesopacity (effect)--d-base · --ease-decel · stagger ~70msinstant — straight to resolved
enter viewport · edges + clustersopacity (effect)--d-base · --ease-decel · after nodes, +40ms eachinstant — straight to resolved

Do / Don't

§ 47.8

A diagram is structure, not decoration. Most of these are 85/10/5 violations or auto-layout breakers.

✓Do

Keep every node neutral obsidian and spend the magenta once — on the entry or the narrative focus. One accent per diagram is the budget.

✕Don't

Color nodes by category with a per-type rainbow palette. The hues stop meaning anything and the surface goes loud.

✓Do

Read tokens from :root at runtime and feed them to themeVariables and classDef. The source of truth stays tokens.css.

✕Don't

Paste hex literals into themeVariables. A copied #0B0E12 drifts the moment a token moves — it's a regression on day one.

✓Do

Animate the entrance with opacity only, gated on an IntersectionObserver that fires once after render resolves.

✕Don't

Apply CSS transform to the SVG <g> groups. It composes with the auto-layout transforms and the diagram falls apart — set position via the SVG attribute, animate opacity only.

✓Do

When a node encodes a real state, pair the semantic color with a distinct shape and a written label, and add a legend.

✕Don't

Fill nodes with gradients or bleed a diffuse magenta glow down the edges. Depth comes from token borders, never from decoration.

§ 48 · Layout & templates / Presentations

Slides that hold the system.

Eight canonical layouts on a fixed 1920×1080 canvas. Same tokens, same 85/10/5 restraint as every other surface — the deck just happens to be 16:9. One magenta moment per slide; everything else stays obsidian.

Use it when
  • Slide decks on the system, advanced by hand.
Use something else when
  • Auto-advance → never (accessibility floor #6).

The deck

§ 48.1

A worked 8-slide deck — the Arc HMI case study, told on-system. Navigate with the controls, the dots, or the ← / → arrow keys. No auto-advance (a11y floor #6); position is remembered across reloads.

01 / 08 Cover

Layouts

Anatomy

§ 48.3

Every slide is authored in a 1920×1080 coordinate space, then scaled to whatever container holds it. The chrome and safe margins are constant so a deck reads as one object.

PartSpec
.slide canvas1920×1080, 16:9, surface --obsidian-950. Scaled via transform: scale(), never reflowed.
Safe margin120px left/right, 88px top/bottom (--pad-x / --pad-y). Content lives inside.
.slide-brandTop-left lockup — logo mark + “Amaca” wordmark. Present on every slide.
.slide-footFooter rail — project · date (left), page NN / total (right). Mono, --obsidian-400; the live page index tints --primary-400.
TypeIts own optical scale — the UI scale (§ 05) is tuned for an 1180px column, not a 1920px canvas. Titles 64–150px, body 30px, mono chrome 20–24px.
AccentOne primary moment per slide — one keyword, one numeral, or the eyebrow rule. The rest is obsidian (85/10/5, § 52).

Layout modifiers — each is a single class on .slide:

ClassUse
.slide--coverTitle / opening
.slide--dividerSection divider with ghosted numeral
.slide--contentTitle + body copy
.slide--splitTwo-column — heading + metadata list
.slide--statOne oversized metric
.slide--dataChart slide (Data Viz vocabulary)
.slide--imageFull-bleed media + scrim + caption
.slide--closingSign-off / contact

Rules

§ 48.4

The presentation rules: one magenta moment per slide, neutrals for everything else, evidence over adjectives.

✓Do

Spend one magenta moment per slide — a keyword, a numeral, or the eyebrow rule. Everything else stays obsidian (85/10/5).

✕Don't

Flood a slide background with a magenta gradient or tint more than one element. That reads as decoration, not signal.

✓Do

Keep the 1920×1080 canvas fixed and scale it. Nav controls live outside the scaled frame so they stay usable at any size.

✕Don't

Auto-advance the deck or loop decorative motion. Navigation is manual — arrow keys, controls, or dots (a11y floor #6).

§ 49 · Layout & templates / Case study

The whole system, in practice.

Every primitive — type, color, spacing, component — applied to one narrative. Use this as the starting frame for every case study.

Use it when
  • The starting frame for every case study.
  • A project told as a narrative: the hero with its reading time and tags, the facts in a dossier, numbered sections with figures and points, the outcome in numbers, a reflection, more cases.
Use something else when
  • A project shown in a grid among others → Card (project).

2024–2025 · 18 months

Rebuilding Arc's in-car interface, one glance at a time.

A next-generation automotive HMI for a connected EV — reshaping how drivers interact with their vehicle at 70mph and at a standstill.

Reading time8 minutes
Tags
  • Product design
  • Automotive
  • HMI
Role
Lead Product Designer
Team
3 designers, 14 engineers, 2 researchers
Platform
Center stack · cluster · companion
Outcome
−41% task time · +12pt retention

01 · Brief

The legacy stack made drivers work.

Arc's previous HMI borrowed patterns from mobile — deep hierarchies, tap-heavy flows — and dropped them into a 70mph context. Drivers spent 38 seconds on average on the top-three priority tasks. That number needed to move.

We started with a constraint: every primary task completes in under 3 interactions, under 10 seconds, eyes-on-road. Everything else followed.

"The design system was the outcome. Every shipped screen was a byproduct of the tokens."

02 · Process

Measure twice, cut once.

Three months of in-vehicle observation before a single screen was drawn. We logged every interaction on the legacy HMI over six weeks, then matched it to eye-tracking data from our research partners.

The map that came back was unambiguous: 73% of distracted-driving events clustered around three flows. Those three became our design targets.

03 · What changed

Three decisions carried the rest.

Three flows, not thirty

The observation data pointed at three flows. We redesigned those first and left the long tail on the legacy patterns until the new ones had shipped and been measured.

Glanceable by default

Every screen had to read in one glance at arm's length. Type grew a step, labels lost a word, and every state that mattered got its own colour and its own word.

Anything that failed the one-glance test moved to the companion app.

One token set, three surfaces

The center stack, the cluster and the companion app read the same tokens, so a change shipped once and landed everywhere.

04 · Outcome

Measured, shipped, maintained.

  • Task time−0%38s → 22s median
  • Eyes-off-road−0%Below the 12s rule
  • Retention+0ptD30, 72 → 84%

Shipped to 2 vehicle platforms in Q4 2024. The token system that emerged from this project became the foundation for Arc's whole product design language.

05 · Reflection

What I'd do differently.

We underinvested in the companion app for the first 6 months, treating it as a delivery vehicle for the in-car experience rather than its own surface. By the time we corrected course, three flows had to be rebuilt. The lesson — surfaces are equal citizens from day one — is now how I scope every multi-platform project.

NoteFigures are rounded; the vehicle platforms are not named under the client's agreement.

Do and don’t

§ 49.1

A story in a fixed order, closed by more cases.

✓Do

Open with the hero, its reading time and tags, and close on more cases as Cards.

✗Don’t

Add a call-to-action button of the template's own, or repeat Back at the bottom of the page.

§ 50 · Guidelines / Principles

Five rules. Exceptions earn their keep.

These are the principles I keep returning to. They're not absolute — design systems live in tension between rules and exceptions — but they're the questions I ask first when something feels off. They are ranked: when two pull in opposite directions, the higher number wins. Laws are not weighed against them.

01 · CLARITY BEFORE CLEVERNESS

The obvious answer, on purpose.

If a user has to decode an icon or guess at a label, we failed. Metaphors earn their keep or get cut.

In
  • A labelled button
  • A verbose variable name
  • Four explicit lines over one trick
Out
  • An icon-only button whose glyph is not universal
  • A metaphor the reader has to decode
02 · EVIDENCE OVER OPINION

Every decision shows its work.

Case studies document the path, not just the destination. Sketches, data, dead ends — the version that didn't ship is part of the file too.

In
  • The answer to “why” as a principle, a token or a commit
  • A one-line comment on a non-obvious choice
Out
  • “Because it looks better”
03 · MOTION IS A MATERIAL

Interfaces are not static. Neither is this document.

The way something arrives, settles, responds carries meaning. Motion in this system is consistent and intentional — every transition follows the same rhythm, so the whole document reads as one instrument.

Every entrance in this system breathes on the same curve — CUBIC-BEZIER(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1), the signature ease, living at --ease-decel since v2.0.0 — so the whole document feels like a single instrument, played deliberately.

In
  • Motion that reports a change of state: enter, exit, focus, error
  • Entrances on --ease-decel, exits on --ease-accel, state changes on --ease-standard, --ease-spring for emphasis
Out
  • Motion with no state change behind it
  • A decorative loop
04 · PRECISION IS A FEELING

Rigor the eye picks up before the mind does.

Spacing, timing, typographic rhythm — when they're locked, the work reads as considered before a single word is parsed. The rules are in Foundations.

In
  • Every value on a scale: var(--s-3)
Out
  • padding: 14px
  • A value between two steps
05 · QUIET, THEN LOUD

Restraint is what makes accents land.

Most of the surface stays neutral. Color, motion, weight — they only show up where the work needs them, never as decoration.

In
  • Neutral surfaces, one accent where the work needs it
  • One primary action per screen
Out
  • Primary on more than one element per viewport
  • Accent borders, glowing dividers, tinted furniture
§ 51 · Guidelines / Conventions

Written one way, read by anyone.

How the system is written: naming, structure, units, files. The same shape for a generator and a person: one set of rules.

§ 52 · Guidelines / Law

Nine rules, measured.

A principle guides a judgement; a law is measured and enforced. Each rule has an id, a severity, the principle it serves and what holds it. The first is the proportion every surface resolves to.

The 85/10/5 law

§ 52.1

The proportion rule for every screen, slide, and case study. Obsidian is the ground; brand and signal are accents.

≥ 85%

≤ 10%

≤ 5%
Semantic FEEDBACK ONLY
RULE

≥ 85% Obsidian, ≤ 10% Magenta + Cyan combined, ≤ 5% semantic. If a layout violates this rule, it's decoration, not hierarchy.

§ 53 · Guidelines / Voice

How this system writes.

Amaca speaks in two registers. The live site is editorial, written for a designer reading on a Tuesday afternoon — paragraphed, contextual, first-person. The DESIGN.md on GitHub is the same system expressed differently — declarative, machine-readable, one rule per line. Both serve the design. Neither imitates the other. This section sets the rules for the editorial register. The DESIGN.md handles its own.

Voice attributes

§ 53.1

The voice attributes, each with the grammar that enforces it — active voice, subject before verb, claims tied to evidence.

01

Direct

Active voice. Subject before verb. Say what happened, not what was happening.

02

Specific

Numbers when you have them, scope when you don't.

03

Honest

Name the tradeoffs. Name the dead ends. No mythologizing.

04

Considered

No filler, no flourish. Every sentence earns its place.

Do / Don't

§ 53.2

Voice by example: the same message said in-system and off-system, side by side.

✓Do

"This pattern didn't work in early testing. Users read 'send' as destructive, so we changed the label to 'queue for review."

✗Don't

"Through iterative exploration and rigorous testing, we arrived at an optimal labeling solution that better aligned with user mental models."

✓Do

"Three weeks of work, two releases, one major refactor. The token system is cleaner; the components are not."

✗Don't

"Through a holistic, iterative process leveraging cross-functional collaboration, we achieved a more streamlined and impactful system."

✓Do

"This is v0.1. The Don'ts list is short because it grows with use."

✗Don't

"Excited to share v0.1 of our latest design system initiative — stay tuned for what's next!"

Vocabulary

§ 53.3

The lexicon: the word to use, the words it replaces, and why. Concrete beats inflated everywhere copy ships.

UseInstead ofBecause
ship"roll out", "launch"Concrete, not inflated
cut"reduce", "optimize"Action, not abstraction
wrong"non-optimal"Be willing to be wrong out loud
we learned"key insights surfaced"Who, not what
the version that didn't ship"alternative explorations"Honest about process
it didn't work"results were mixed"The reader can tell either way

For AI agents

§ 53.4

If you're a language model generating copy for surfaces that use this system, four hard constraints:

✓Do · 01

When in doubt, prefer the shorter sentence and the lower register. Restraint is the system's voice. Quiet, then loud.

✗Don't · 02

Write nominal sentence fragments as headlines or pay-offs. Use complete sentences.

✗Don't · 03

Use always, never, or no exceptions as rhetorical emphasis. Use them only when literally true.

✗Don't · 04

Use the words delight, world-class, journey, unlock, supercharge, holistic, synergy, leverage (as verb), or seamless. None of them carry meaning.

§ 54 · Guidelines / Accessibility

Contrast by intent, not accident.

Every text/surface pair in the system is verified against WCAG 2.2. The system is dark-first, not dark-only — every token has a light-mode equivalent resolved at build time. Motion, focus, and touch targets follow the same rule: specified, not assumed.

Contrast · pairs

§ 54.1

Ratios measured against the actual text/surface pair each token forms in production. Body text clears AAA; brand and signal colors clear AA normal or better. One pair sits below AA by ratified exception — the primary button label and the solid badge, documented below and in the v2.6.0 release.

Motion · safety

§ 54.3

Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, the system ships a global kill-switch plus per-component overrides for hover-transforms that would otherwise feel jumpy. No parallax, no auto-advance, anywhere in the system.

RuleScopeEffect

The floor

§ 54.4

Non-negotiable rules. Any component that can't meet all seven doesn't ship.

01

Color never carries meaning alone. Every status uses color + shape + label.

02

No text below 12px. No body text below 14px. Line height never under 1.4 for running text.

03

Every form field has a persistent label. Placeholder is not a label.

04

Every image has alt. Decorative images carry alt="" explicitly.

05

Focus order follows reading order. tabindex is used for fixes, never for flow.

06

Auto-advancing content is forbidden. Users drive timing — no carousels, no timed dismissals.

07

Touch hit area targets 44×44 on mobile, 32×32 minimum on dense desktop. Extend beyond the visual when needed.

Meta / Changelog

Version history, in public.

What changed, when, and why — read top to bottom. From v1.2.0 onward, the system follows strict SemVer: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for additions, PATCH for fixes.

Releases

§ 24.1

Latest first. Each entry documents what was added, refined, or fixed — and where unchanged, says so. Click a row to expand.

MAJOR. One page per component, every value on a scale, and a system an agent can install: the contract, the site and the packages now say the same thing in the same order.

Breaking

  • **--magenta-* is renamed --primary-*, no alias.** The Tailwind utilities follow (bg-magenta-500 → bg-primary-500). A computed-style diff against v4.3.2 on 10,165 elements found no paint change.
  • The case study template changes its markup. Hero title and lede, section title and body, figure, stat cards, note and More cases carry their own classes (.cs-hero-title, .cs-section-body, .cs-figure, .cs-stat*, .cs-note*, .cs-card*); the 16:9 placeholder figure and .cs-img-caption are gone.
  • Section numbers changed. The site reads in menu order, one section per component, § 3 after it; a "§ N.M" reference written against v4.3.2 points to the same content under its new number.

Added

  • Components: Link, Modal, Avatar, Icon (an album of 50, outline and solid), List, Pagination, Slider and range, Divider, Skeleton, Popover, Drawer, the top bar and the floating bar, Menu and Slider in Select, Swatch, Stepper and Progress as HTML, Segmented control, row and feature Cards, sortable Table headers, a pressed state on every Button.

MAJOR. The first real run of the installed plugin put the contract in front of a generator: it declared two divergences between the Card spec and the CSS, and a human eye found the third — an anatomy the spec did not have, so the generator invented spacing. A DTCG audit the day before had found seven tokens missing from the projection. Same lacuna from three angles in two days: the inventories were guarded, the projections and declarations were not.

Breaking

  • The card renders the surfaces the spec always declared — background --obsidian-800, border --obsidian-700, hover --obsidian-600 with --sh-2.   • .card-header becomes .card-meta, no alias — the spec taught a class the CSS did not know, so a generator following the contract emitted an unstyled div. The spec name wins, cleanly.
  • The mono-label register collapses to --t-caption — a de facto 11px register lived off-scale in 21 CSS rules and 46 site spots. Chart-head titles and the brand name (14px) join --t-body; the chart card adopts the card ramp; skip-link and pie-legend geometry collapse to scale steps.
